Close TCP server on exceptions

When running a command like `pymobiledevice3 developer debugserver start-server 3921` with tunneld, it first tries without tunneld, raise an exception, which climbs back up in the call stack, bypassing the closing of the socket, leading the next attempt to fail as the port is set and that the previous server has never been closed.
This commit fixes that issue.

Add monitor-single command for continuous process monitoring

This command allows monitoring processes with configurable interval and duration parameters. Features include:
- Continuous monitoring of process metrics (CPU, memory, etc.)
- Configurable polling interval via -i/--interval option
- Optional duration limit via -d/--duration option
- Filter processes by attribute via -a/--attributes option
- Output to file in JSONL format via -o/--output option
- UTC timestamp output for each snapshot
- Multiple filters on same attribute use OR logic (e.g., -a name=App1 -a name=App2)
- Filters on different attributes use AND logic (e.g., -a name=App1 -a pid=123)
- Respects user color choice via print_json

dvt: Add initial support for XCTest on iOS 17+

Main changes:
  - xcuitest.py: use AppService to spawn the TestRunner
  - xcuitest.py: sned test configuration via the DTX channel
  - remote_server.py: user negative channel codes for reverse channels
  - remote_server.py: add XCTCapabilities
  - remote_server.py: thread-safe ( not strictly necessary )
  - cli/developer/dvt/__init__.py: added `--env` option

Add support to run tests on iOS 17+ devices using the new Tunnel
communication channel and servigin the test_configuration through
the Tunnel instead of using a file on the device.

To make this work, it was key to add support for reverse channels,
in particular, when receiving the `_requestChannelWithCode:identifier:`
method call, the channel number to use in subsequent communication is
the inverted integer received (e.g. if `code==1` we're going to use `channelCode=-1`).

That channel is then used to send the `_IDE_startExecutingTestPlanWithProtocolVersion:`
remote server method call, which start the test plan.

Last but not least, was the feature of providing the `XCTestConfiguration`
via the Tunnel (as return value to a remote method call) instead of using
a file on the device.

As I was spawning background threads to monitor the background channels,
I had to make the remote_server thread-safe, although it wasn't strictly
required for CLI usage.

I've tried to keep the logic and data structures unchanged for devices
that runs iOS < 17, except for the consumption of the test output, which
has been removed as we have to authorize the test before receiving any output.

Tested on iPhone SE (2020) [iPhone12,8] with iOS 26.1 .
Tested on iPhone 11 [iPhone12,1] with iOS 16.5 .

service_connection: fix BrokenPipeError after SSL upgrade via start_tls()

The refactored ssl_start() called _ensure_started() to create plain
reader/writer, then upgraded via writer.start_tls(). After start_tls(),
writer._transport is replaced with the new _SSLProtocolTransport, but
reader._transport still points at the old closed _SelectorSocketTransport.
Subsequent reads/writes hit mismatched transports, causing BrokenPipeError
or IncompleteReadError.

Fix: use two paths depending on whether the socket is already registered
with the event loop:
- Not yet started: asyncio.open_connection(ssl=...) creates both reader
  and writer SSL-aware from the start.
- Already started (e.g. mid-session SSL upgrade in lockdown): the socket
  is already registered so open_connection() would raise RuntimeError;
  keep writer.start_tls() for this case.

Thanks to @tux-mind!

DTX: implementat based on other open srouce projects

A new implementation of Apple's DTX binary full-duplex multiplexing
protocol, mainly used by XCode.

I've take inspiration from [go-ios], [frida-core] and [idb].
None of these projects had a full implementation ( the best one was frida ),
so this task was quite challenging.

[go-ios]: https://github.com/danielpaulus/go-ios
[frida-core]: https://github.com/frida/frida-core/blob/e5e30334152b48dddc16c4af3c678cc19e0ca1b6/src/fruity/dtx.vala
[idb]: https://github.com/facebook/idb

fix: register XCTest services early to fix xcuitest over RSD tunnels

When using xcuitest through a RemotePairing (RSD) tunnel — e.g. via
Tailscale over a non-local network — the device sends DTX messages
(notably `_XCT_testRunnerReadyWithCapabilities:`) before the
`DtxProxyService.connect()` call has a chance to register the service
classes. The messages fall through to `DTXDynamicService`, which does
not implement the callback, causing the connection to terminate.

This did not affect lockdown (USB) tunnels because of lower latency,
but is reliably reproducible over higher-latency RSD tunnels.

Adding `REGISTER_SERVICES` to `_TestManagerProvider` ensures
`XCTestManager_IDEInterface`, `XCTestManager_DaemonConnectionInterface`,
and `XCTestDriverInterface` are registered during `DtxServiceProvider.connect()`,
before the DTX handshake completes and the device starts sending messages.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

xcuitest: fix DYLD env vars passed to test runner on iOS 17+

Two bugs in _generate_launch_args that mostly affected iOS 17+ but
hadn't surfaced visibly until iOS 26.4.2 made the cost more severe:

1) Literal "$" in f-strings, not shell expansion

   app_env["DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH"] = f"${app_env['DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH']}/System/Developer/Library/Frameworks:"

   Python f-strings substitute via {x}, not ${x}. The leading $ is a
   literal character. iOS launchd does not shell-expand env vars, so
   the resulting DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH and DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH start with
   a stray $, e.g.

     $/private/var/containers/.../Frameworks:/System/Developer/Library/Frameworks:

   dyld tolerates this on older iOS (skipping the malformed first
   entry), but on iOS 26 the bad prefix can cascade into
   XCTAutomationSupport.framework failing to resolve, and the test
   runner aborts inside +[XCTRunnerDaemonSession sharedSession] with
   SIGABRT.

2) DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES points at a path emptied on iOS 17+

   app_env["DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES"] = "/Developer/usr/lib/libMainThreadChecker.dylib"

   Apple moved the developer libs from /Developer/usr/lib/ to
   /System/Developer/usr/lib/ on iOS 17+, and libMainThreadChecker.dylib
   is no longer shipped to devices at all. Inserting a non-existent
   dylib is at best a no-op + dyld warning; gate the insert on
   product_major_version < 17 so we just stop adding it on modern iOS.

## Reproduction (before this PR)

  - Device:      iPhone 17 Pro Max, iOS 26.4.2 (build 23E261)
  - pymd3:       9.12.1
  - WDA bundle:  appium/WebDriverAgent master, sideloaded via Flexstore
  - Command:     pymobiledevice3 developer dvt xcuitest com.facebook.WebDriverAgentRunner.xctrunner
  - Result:      WebDriverAgentRunner-Runner-*.ips crash with
                 "+[XCTRunnerDaemonSession sharedSession] +316 →
                 NSAssertion → abort()" exactly 1.x seconds after launch.

Verified independently in doronz88/pymobiledevice3#1666 comment 2 by
@JulesGosnell on iPhone 14 / iOS 26.4.2.

## After this PR

DTX session progresses through ctrl session init, main session init,
launch_suspended_process (test runner gets a real PID), and
_IDE_authorizeTestSessionWithProcessID_ (returns True). The remaining
iOS-26-specific failure is at the reverse XCTestDriverInterface
proxy step — that one looks like a separate iOS 26 testmanagerd
change, tracked in #1666 and outside the scope of this PR.

## What this PR does NOT claim to fix

This PR does not unblock real test runs on iOS 26.4.2 by itself. It
fixes two long-standing, demonstrably wrong env-var values that were
masked by dyld's tolerance on older iOS, and it cleans up the launch
path so the remaining iOS-26-only failure can be analyzed without
the noise of the DYLD bugs in the way. Related: #1666.

core_device: CoreDeviceService.invoke accepts an action_identifier

``actionIdentifier`` field alongside the message type. Every
new service implementation that follows (HID, display, etc.) needs
to set it to the action-specific identifier (e.g.
``com.apple.coredevice.action.mediastreamstart``); the existing
``invoke()`` helper was hardcoded and forced callers to bypass it
for any non-default action. Pass it through.

core_device: IndigoHIDService + UniversalHIDServiceService + HID CLI

Two HID-related RemoteXPC services exposed by ``dtuhidd``:

  - IndigoHIDService (``com.apple.coredevice.hid.indigo``) -- delivers
    a single hardware-button state change (Home, Power, Volume,
    Mute, Siri, etc.). Wire format uses the
    ``IndigoButtonEvent`` envelope with usage_page + usage_code +
    state (down/up/canceled). Other Indigo event kinds (keyboard,
    scroll, vendor-defined) use Apple's Mercury peer-event envelope,
    which has not been reverse-engineered yet -- documented inline.

  - UniversalHIDServiceService
    (``com.apple.coredevice.hid.universalhidservice``) -- exposes the
    device's already-registered HID surfaces (touchscreen,
    trackpad-style gesture surface, mainScreenButtons). Carries raw
    HID reports to a specific _ServiceID. Wire formats sniffed from
    Xcode-mirror sessions and documented inline:
      * mainTouchscreen (rid=0x09, 58 bytes, _ServiceID 257)
      * touchscreenGesture (rid=0x13, 19 bytes, _ServiceID 1281)

    Both surfaces require an active media stream to flip their
    backboardd-side auth gate; ``touch_session`` is the async-context
    helper that opens a video stream just to hold that gate open.

CLI:
  - hid {button,raw-button}
  - universal-hid-service {list-connected,send-report,tap,drag,
                           swipe,session}

Tap/drag/swipe coords are UInt16 (0..65535) normalised across the
display; ``session`` reads multi-gesture scripts from stdin / a file
inside ONE media-stream open (faster + survives bursty input).

core_device: DisplayService + media_stream_offer + display CLI

device's media-stream subsystem
(``com.apple.coredevice.displayservice``):

  - start_video_stream / start_audio_stream / stop_media_stream

core_device: serve-web (browser HEVC viewer via WebCodecs)

Live screen mirror for any modern browser. Decode happens in-browser
through the W3C WebCodecs VideoDecoder; the server forwards Annex-B
HEVC bytes verbatim plus a small companion JS viewer.

Pipeline:
    device → UDP/RTP/HEVC → asyncio depacketize → HTTP chunked
           → browser VideoDecoder → <canvas>

Surfaces:
  - screen_stream.py: ScreenStreamServer (web UI, /stream.bin video
    chunks, /audio.bin pre-decoded PCM via AAC-ELD, /touch and
    /button input forwarded back to the device's HID stack, /restart
    + /codec for manual recovery). Captures helpers
    capture_rtp_to_file / capture_audio_rtp_to_file are exposed for
    the start-video-stream / start-audio-stream CLIs.
  - aac_eld.py: AudioToolbox AAC-ELD -> s16le 48kHz stereo PCM
    decoder (macOS only, pure ctypes); raises clearly elsewhere.
  - hevc_phantom.py: synthesise phantom NALs so the browser's
    decoder doesn't stall on bootstrap POC gaps.
  - misc/rtp_dump.py: convert captured RTP into Annex-B .h265.

The web viewer survives:
  - bootstrap before the device has emitted an IDR (phantom NALs)
  - RTP packet loss (PLI-driven IDR re-request)
  - WebCodecs LTRP staleness under motion (decoder-rebuild loop)
  - audio session reaping (RTCP RR keepalive)
  - dropped HID dispatch under load (queue + keep-alive)
  - manual restart from the viewer

CLI:
  - display serve-web --bind --http-port [--no-audio]
  - display start-video-stream / start-audio-stream (RTP capture)

core_device: serve-vnc (RFB 3.8 server for macOS Screen Sharing)

Live screen mirror exposed as a standard VNC server. macOS Finder
⌘K → vnc://127.0.0.1:5901 opens Screen Sharing.app directly against
the device. No browser, no WebCodecs, no canvas state to corrupt --
each framebuffer update is a fresh BGRA frame straight from the host
VideoToolbox HEVC decoder.

Pipeline:
    device → UDP/RTP/HEVC → asyncio depacketize
           → VTDecompressionSession (BGRA output) → RFB Raw

No JPEG round-trip on the wire: pixels read directly out of the
CVPixelBuffer and shipped as one full-frame Raw rect per
FramebufferUpdate.

Surfaces:
  - vnc_server.py: VncStreamServer (RFB 3.3 / 3.8 handshake, VNC-Auth
    accept-any-password for the macOS dialog, mandatory Raw encoding,
    decoder-refresh loop, PLI/RTCP feedback, multi-client safe).
  - vt_jpeg.py: HEVCDecoder + HevcToBgraTranscoder -- pure-ctypes
    VideoToolbox wrapper that pins decoder output to 32-bit BGRA so
    we never need a re-encode. Import-safe on non-Darwin (the macOS
    framework loads are behind a sys.platform guard; classes raise a
    clear "requires macOS" RuntimeError if constructed elsewhere).
  - audio_player.py: pure-ctypes CoreAudio AudioQueue PCM playback.
    Same non-Darwin import-safety pattern.

Tears under motion are handled the same way a browser reload handles
them: send RTCP PLI, tear the VT decoder down, rebuild from the new
IDR. Triggers: motion-settled, during sustained motion (active),
idle heartbeat, and once per new VNC client connect.

Input:
  - Left mouse click             -> touchscreen contact
  - Right mouse click            -> Home button
  - Middle mouse click           -> Lock / Power
  - Ctrl+H / Ctrl+L              -> Home / Lock
  - Ctrl+[ / Ctrl+]              -> Volume Down / Up
  - Ctrl+\\ / Ctrl+S             -> Mute / Siri
  - Plain letters are reserved for the upcoming HID text-input path
    -- the CoreDevice "keyboard" surface accepts reports but UIKit
    silently drops them; the wire format gating it (Apple's Mercury
    peer-event envelope / Universal Control) is undocumented.

Audio is off by default; pass --audio to decode the device's AAC-ELD
stream through CoreAudio and play out the host Mac's speakers. RFB
has no audio extension that Screen Sharing.app supports, so playback
is host-local.

CLI:
  - display serve-vnc --bind --port [--audio]

serve-vnc: sticky keyframe-required recovery from VT decode errors

VT silently concealing frames (FrameDropped infoFlag with OSStatus=0)
left serve-vnc relying on the motion/heartbeat refresh loop alone --
worst case a 10 s freeze before the next PLI. Surface the VT error
signal up to a libwebrtc-style two-condition sticky-PLI re-arm:
clears only when an IDR was fed AND a clean frame decoded after it,
with a 500 ms post-IDR grace so queued pre-IDR P-frames don't trigger
a PLI storm. Caps at 8 PLI attempts before giving up and falling back
to the existing motion/heartbeat path.

Adapted from iSharScreen's FrameQualityGate, single-tile.

serve-vnc: proactive PLI on RPS reference-not-in-DPB

VT silently conceals a P-slice when its short-term Reference Picture
Set lists a POC not in the decoder's DPB -- the visible tear case
that doesn't trip OSStatus or FrameDropped. Parse the slice header
ourselves before feeding VT and arm sticky recovery the moment we
spot a missing reference. One frame ahead of any decoder-side
signal, and catches the silent-conceal case where VT never errors.

New ``hevc_rps`` module (single-tile port of iSharScreen's
``proxy/media/hevc_rps.py``). Wired into ``vnc_server``'s recv
loop: feed_sps on SPS NALs, check_slice/commit_decoded around
each AU's feed, reset on transcoder rebuild.

Validated against a live device: SPS parses cleanly, 225 idle
slices in 4s yield no false-positive missing-ref events; POC
sequence comes out 0, 1, 2, ... as expected.

serve-vnc: libav decoder fallback + --decoder CLI flag

VideoToolbox stays the macOS default (HW-accelerated, no GIL
pressure on the audio path). New ``hevc_av`` module wraps
PyAV / libavcodec as the cross-platform fallback for Linux /
Windows hosts where VideoToolbox isn't available. PyAV is an
optional dep; the module raises a clear install hint if it's
needed but missing.

Decoder resolution lives in ``_resolve_decoder``, called per
``VncStreamServer`` constructor:
  - ``auto`` (default): VT on macOS, libav elsewhere.
  - ``vt``: force VideoToolbox (macOS only).
  - ``av``: force PyAV / libav.

``PYMD3_HEVC_DECODER=av`` env var has the same effect as
``--decoder av`` for the auto path.

Same ``feed`` / ``on_frame`` / ``on_decode_error`` / ``width`` /
``height`` / ``close`` surface so the sticky-keyframe recovery
and RPS pre-decode check from the prior two commits keep working
unchanged on either path.

serve-web: active-motion refresh + lightweight /pli recovery path

Close the recovery gap with serve-vnc.

Active-motion refresh: the decoder-refresh loop now also fires
during sustained motion every 1.5 s, not just on motion-settled +
heartbeat. Previously a long scroll could accumulate tears for up
to 10 s (the heartbeat) before the next refresh; now it's capped
at ~1.5 s, matching serve-vnc.

Browser /pli on post-bootstrap decode errors: when WebCodecs throws
after the first few frames, the browser used to just set
needsResync and wait for whatever next IDR happened to arrive
(motion-settled / heartbeat -- potentially seconds later). Now it
hits a new /pli endpoint that fires a single RTCP PLI without
restarting the DisplayService session. Fresh IDR back in
~100-300 ms instead of seconds. /restart stays as the heavier
bootstrap-failure self-heal.

serve-web: side-mounted button layout + Ctrl hotkeys + utility tray

Reorganises the browser viewer's controls around the device's
physical layout so the on-screen UI mirrors the iPhone:

  Left flank   : Mute / Vol + / Vol -
  Right flank  : Power / Lock / Sleep / Siri
  Bottom row   : Home
  Top-right    : Enable Sound / Forced Reset / Force Restart
                 (low-frequency utility controls)

Ctrl-hotkeys mirror serve-vnc's ``_CTRL_COMBO_TO_HID``:
  Ctrl+H = Home, Ctrl+L = Lock, Ctrl+[ = Vol Down,
  Ctrl+] = Vol Up, Ctrl+\\ = Mute, Ctrl+S = Siri.
Tooltips on the affected buttons advertise their shortcut.

Status overlay stays pinned top-left but narrowed to 220 px so it
doesn't reach into the Vol / Mute column. Falls back to the old
flat-wrap layout under 700 px width so phone-sized browsers still
work.

VIEWER_HTML flips from bytes-literal to str + ``.encode("utf-8")``
since the file now carries non-ASCII glyphs (em-dashes in JS
comments).

serve-web: add Swipe ← / Swipe → buttons

Synthesised in the browser: contact at the start edge, 10
intermediate contact samples along the path, release at the end
edge. ~200 ms total so iOS reads it as a real horizontal swipe
(faster gets misread as a flick, slower as a drag). Y stays at
the vertical midpoint; X sweeps nearly edge-to-edge.

Both buttons sit in the bottom row alongside Home, since they're
device-screen gestures rather than hardware-button presses.

core-device: virtual HID keyboard surface (CLI + serve-vnc + serve-web)

dtuhidd exposes a `createService` call on the universalhidservice
RemoteXPC feature: pass a Generic-Desktop-Keyboard report descriptor +
`UniversalControlVirtualService=True` + a chosen `_ServiceID`, get back
that ID, then post 39-byte rid=0x01 reports to it. Decoded from a sniff
of macOS Universal Control mirroring a Keychron keyboard onto the
device, byte-exact-verified against the captured `a`-keydown frame.

Wire format (39 B): `[rid=0x01][30-byte usage bitmap][6-byte Mach-abs
timestamp LE][0x00 0x00]`. Bit `u%8` of byte `1 + u//8` set ⇔ HID
Keyboard usage `u` held. Every report carries the full pressed set --
releases resend with the bit cleared.

`createService` payload quirks (each one cost a round-trip to
narrow down via dtuhidd's syslog `DecodingError` messages):

  - `PrimaryUsage`/`PrimaryUsagePage` are UInt64 at the top level,
    Int64 inside the storage block.
  - `ProductID`/`VendorID`/`DeviceUsage*` are Int64 everywhere.
  - `_ServiceID` is UInt64 everywhere.
  - `Manufacturer`/`ReportDescriptor`/`UniversalControlVirtualService`/
    `Transport` live ONLY under `_CoreDevice_codablePropertyStorage`.
  - Every value inside that storage block is wrapped in a Swift-Codable
    type envelope (`{"bool": ...}` / `{"int": ...}` / `{"string": ...}`
    / `{"data": ...}` / `{"array": [...]}` / `{"dictionary": {...}}` /
    `{"uint": ...}`) -- raw bools/ints under that key get rejected with
    "DecodingError.typeMismatch: dictionary required here".

open, so `create_keyboard_service` is a one-liner inside any
already-authenticated session.

- `cli/developer/core_device.py`: `universal-hid-service type "..."`

Verified end-to-end against a real device: `type abc` exits cleanly
after registering the surface (`Service unknown(0x100002001):
Activated with HID service ID ...` in dtuhidd's syslog) and dispatching
6 reports.

core-device: per-button hold time for IndigoButtonEvent presses

`_handle_button` (serve-web) and the `hid button` CLI both sent the
DOWN and UP IndigoButtonEvents back-to-back -- dtuhidd's own log shows
the two `Handling IndigoButtonEvent` lines ~70 µs apart for our pair,
which backboardd treats as bounce noise for any button that semantically
requires a hold. Home (Consumer/Menu = tap) fired anyway; Lock
(Consumer/Power = sleep on hold) and Siri (Consumer/Voice Command =
start listening on hold) silently no-op'd.

hold_seconds)`, sleep `hold_seconds` between DOWN and UP. Default
0.05 s for tap-class buttons (long enough to clear debounce, short
enough to feel instant), 0.5 s for Lock (empirically sleeps the
device), 1.0 s for Siri (empirically starts listening). The CLI's
`hid button` and serve-web's `/button press` both pick up the
per-button hold from the table; `--state down` / `--state up` paths
are unaffected.

VNC's Ctrl-hotkey path already gets a natural hold from the user's
actual keypress duration, so no change there.

uses with a 0.5 s hold; sending it with a 0.05 s tap is bounce noise
that iOS ignores, so it had no observable behavior. Sleep
(Consumer/0x32) had no observed iOS effect at any hold duration tried
here -- iOS routes the sleep action through the same Power
(Consumer/0x30) hold path that Lock now handles.

Remove both from `_NAMED_BUTTONS` (CLI + serve-web) and drop the two
`<button>` elements from the viewer's right-side cluster. Lock remains
as the single "put the device to sleep" entry point.

serve-web: add cosmetic iPhone bezel around the canvas

A pure-CSS rounded-rect bezel wraps the video canvas, with a `Frame`
toggle in the util-tray (preference persisted in localStorage). No
device-model awareness -- the frame just hugs whatever aspect ratio
the canvas ends up at. Input mapping is unchanged.

serve-web: release stuck contact when pointer-up happens outside the canvas

Pointer capture is supposed to keep pointerup routed back to the
canvas even outside its bounds, but the browser silently drops capture
on window blur / Cmd-Tab / right-click menu / OS interruptions. The up
event then dispatches to whatever element the cursor sits on, our
canvas-only listener never fires, and the contact stays "held"
device-side.

Mirror pointermove/up/cancel listeners onto `window`, add a
`lostpointercapture` backstop, and treat window blur /
visibilitychange as implicit releases. Cache the last known coords so
the synthetic release has a sensible position even when triggered
without an event.

serve-web: size the canvas by devicePixelRatio so 1:1 backing pixels stay crisp

CSS max-width/max-height forced the browser to bilinear-downscale the
~1264x2752 source to fit the viewport, which softened text and UI.
Drop the CSS caps and let JS (`fitCanvasToViewport`) size the canvas
in CSS pixels at `backing-store / devicePixelRatio`: on a Retina
display each backing pixel lands on exactly one device pixel = the
crisp 1:1 look, while still fitting inside the viewport.

If even the DPR-divided size doesn't fit we shrink proportionally;
`image-rendering: high-quality` keeps that fallback path from going
visibly blocky in Chrome.

serve-web: extract HTML/CSS/JS into resource files

`screen_stream.py` carried the entire viewer page as a ~760-line raw
string literal -- comfortable to write inline but impossible to edit
with proper syntax highlighting or linting. Move the markup, styling,
and decoder/input/audio JS into separate files under
`pymobiledevice3/resources/serve_web/`, load them via
`importlib.resources` (matching the pattern used by
`automation_session.py`), and add `/viewer.css` / `/viewer.js` routes
to the existing HTTP server. The `__AUDIO_DEFAULT_ON__` per-request
substitution now happens on the JS bytes (where the placeholder
lives) instead of the HTML. Behaviour is unchanged.

media_stream_offer: replace verbatim hex templates with a protobuf builder

The video + audio mediaBlob templates were 5-byte-replaceable hex
literals captured verbatim from Xcode -- impossible to tweak any field
other than `session_id` without re-capturing.

Reverse-engineer the protobuf schema (cross-referenced against
iShareScreen's AVConference-port) and replace the templates with named
constructors. Defaults reproduce the captured templates byte-for-byte
(asserted by the new `_self_check`, runnable via `python -m
pymobiledevice3.remote.core_device.media_stream_offer`); kwargs expose
the negotiation knobs we'd previously been unable to touch -- notably
the protobuf-level `ltrpEnabled` and `allowRTCPFB` flags. The outer
options-dict equivalents were confirmed ignored by the daemon; these
inner-blob flags haven't been probed yet.

serve-web/serve-vnc: expose ltrpEnabled / allowRTCPFB negotiation knobs

The protobuf-level switches reverse-engineered in the previous commit
were reachable from Python but not from the CLI. Plumb them through
`DisplayService.start_video_stream` (new kwargs), the
`ScreenStreamServer` / `VncStreamServer` constructors, and finally
two `--no-ltrp` / `--rtcp-fb` flags on each of `serve-web` and
`serve-vnc`.

Defaults preserve the existing captured-Xcode behaviour. These are
explicit experiment flags -- `--no-ltrp` should kill the mid-stream
LTRP-driven tearing on iPhone (memory: `project_hevc_motion_tears`),
and `--rtcp-fb` invites the device to close the open-loop rate
control loop (memory: `project_avcrc_ignores_rr`).

serve-web/serve-vnc: default ltrpEnabled=False after on-device probe

On-device probing (iPhone18,4 iOS 27.0) confirmed the protobuf-level
`ltrpEnabled` switch is HONOURED by the device -- setting field 7 to 0
in VideoSettings yields `IsltrpEnabled: false` in the response's
streamConfig. The earlier "LTRP is forced on" memory note was about
the outer options dict; the inner mediaBlob field is a different code
path that actually flows into the encoder.

LTRP-off should eliminate the mid-stream tearing pattern under UDP
loss (no FEC/RTX, occasional loss): with LTRP on, a partially-lost
long-term reference frame stays corrupted for the rest of the GOP;
with LTRP off, references slide forward and corruption self-clears.

Flip the default everywhere (mediaBlob builder, DisplayService,
ScreenStreamServer, VncStreamServer). The CLI now exposes `--ltrp` to
opt back into the captured-Xcode behaviour for regression testing,
replacing the previous `--no-ltrp` (which is moot when LTRP is
already off by default). `--rtcp-fb` stays opt-in.

Also probed (negative results, logged so we don't re-walk them):
- Setting `f4=width` / `f5=height` inside VideoSettings of the offer
  is silently ignored -- the device returns panel-native 1264x2736
  regardless. Those fields are device->client only.
- `allow_rtcp_fb=True` produces no observable change in streamConfig.

media_stream_offer: map VideoSettings field numbers; add fec/tiles kwargs

Recovered the full field-number → property-name mapping for
VCMediaNegotiationBlobVideoSettings by dumping the __objc_methname
table at 0x83c381..0x83c463 (the 14 properties live in adjacent slots,
and offset order matches proto field-tag order against every
previously-verified anchor: f1=SSRC, f2=allowRTCPFB, f3=banks,
f4=customVideoWidth, f5=customVideoHeight, f7=ltrpEnabled,
f12=blackFrameOnClearScreenEnabled all match).

The new map gives us f6=tilesPerFrame, f8=pixelFormats,
f9=hdrModesSupported, f10=fecEnabled, f11=rtxEnabled,
f13=foveationSupported, f14=enableInterleavedEncoding -- expose
fec_enabled and tiles_per_frame as kwargs on build_media_blob_video()
and DisplayService.start_video_stream().

On-device probe results (iPhone18,4 iOS 27.0):

- fec_enabled=True: ACCEPTED by the device (not Invalid Parameter)
  but no echo in the answer's VideoSettings and no fecEnabled key in
  streamConfig. Either silently honoured or silently dropped.
- rtx_enabled=True: REJECTED with Invalid Parameter. The
  screen-blob path likely requires separate localRTXSSRC/remoteRTXSSRC
  fields (referenced in AVConference VCVideoStream logs).
- tiles_per_frame=4: ACCEPTED but ignored. The device negotiates AVC
  over our HEVC bank (probably because our HEVC feature string is too
  sparse), and AVC doesn't support tile-level parallelism.

Defaults all left off -- these are research knobs, not perf wins.
The user-visible motion tears at heavy interaction are most likely
the bitrate-cap-driven QP escalation already captured in
project_displayservice_bitrate_cap, not something a negotiation knob
can fix.

media_stream_offer: default fecEnabled=True

The device accepts `f10=fecEnabled` in the offer without rejecting it
(unlike `f11=rtxEnabled` which returns Invalid Parameter), but the
answer doesn't echo it back and `streamConfig` has no `fecEnabled`
key, so we can't observe whether the encoder is actually emitting FEC
NALs. The risk of flipping the default is therefore low (the device
clearly tolerates it) and the potential upside is non-zero (if it
silently honours the request, lost UDP packets get repaired and motion
tears improve). Worst case it's a no-op.

`--no-fec` is not exposed on the CLI yet -- users wanting to test
without FEC can pass `fec_enabled=False` via the Python API.

serve-web/serve-vnc: default --bind to 0.0.0.0

Both viewers are tools the user wants reachable from other devices on
their LAN -- defaulting to 127.0.0.1 forced an explicit `--bind
0.0.0.0` every time. Flip the default. Help text now spells out the
security implication: the HTTP `/touch /button /key` endpoints have
no auth, the VNC server has no password, so anyone reaching the port
can both watch and control the iPhone. Pass `--bind 127.0.0.1` to
restore the old behaviour.

serve-web: add --https option with an ephemeral self-signed cert

WebCodecs is gated on a secure context: browsers refuse to expose the
API on plain http:// from any non-loopback origin. Accessing serve-web
from another LAN host therefore fails with `isConfigSupported threw`
before a single frame can decode.

Generate an ed25519 self-signed cert on startup (SANs cover localhost,
::1, 127.0.0.1, and the bind address when concrete), load it into an
`ssl.SSLContext` via a tempfile that's unlinked as soon as the context
has loaded the PEM, and pass `ssl=` to `asyncio.start_server`. The
browser warns on first visit, the user accepts, and WebCodecs unlocks.

CLI: `--https`. Default off so the localhost-only case stays plain
http (no cert warning prompt).

serve-web: cert SANs now cover all local interface IPs when --bind 0.0.0.0

Previously the self-signed cert's SAN list was just the three loopback
entries when `--bind 0.0.0.0`, so connecting to https://<lan-ip>:port/
from another machine produced a CN/SAN mismatch the browser would
either reject outright (Safari) or render as a clickable warning
(Chrome). Some browsers won't click-through self-signed mismatches at
all on a public-IP-looking target.

When bind is the wildcard, enumerate every local interface IP via
`getaddrinfo(gethostname(), ...)` plus a UDP `connect()` probe for the
default route's local address, and add each as a SAN. The browser now
gets a cert that actually claims to be the host the user typed.

serve-web: switch self-signed cert from ed25519 to RSA-2048

Chrome and Safari handle ed25519 server certs inconsistently in 2026
-- some builds reject them with "connection unexpectedly closed"
during the TLS handshake, no actionable browser warning. RSA-2048 is
universally accepted at the cost of a slightly slower generate (still
<200 ms on a modern Mac, once per server start).

core-device: add OrientationService + 'rotate' CLI

Decoded from a Xcode-mirror sniff of four back-to-back rotate-left clicks.
Each request is an OrientationRequest envelope on the new
'com.apple.coredevice.devicecontrol' RemoteXPC service:

    {featureIdentifier: 'com.apple.coredevice.feature.remote.devicecontrol.orientation',
     messageType: 'OrientationRequest',
     payload: {rotate: {_0: 'left'}}}

The reply carries currentDeviceOrientation + currentDeviceNonFlatOrientation
+ currentDeviceOrientationLocked. Four 'left' requests cycle the device
through portrait -> landscapeLeft -> portraitUpsideDown -> landscapeRight.

Exposed as 'pymobiledevice3 developer core-device rotate [left|right]'.

serve-web: device rotation buttons + canvas-internal rotation

Adds Rotate ↺ / Rotate ↻ buttons in the viewer's util-tray and a
POST /rotate endpoint on the server that forwards to
OrientationService.rotate(direction).

The rotation is applied INSIDE the canvas (ctx.translate + ctx.rotate
+ drawImage on each frame), not via CSS transform on the canvas
element, so the canvas's own CSS box matches the rotated footprint
and the surrounding flex layout + cosmetic bezel wrap it naturally —
no overflow, no separate bezel rotation.

drawPending watches the buffer's aspect ratio; if it flips between
portrait and landscape (i.e. iOS is re-rendering for the new
orientation) the in-canvas rotation auto-resets to 0 so we don't
double-rotate already-oriented content. Touch coordinates project
through the inverse rotation back into the device buffer's frame
before normalising to HID 0..65535.

serve-web: 'Keyboard: on/off' toggle to release host keystrokes

New util-tray button that pauses keydown/keyup forwarding so the
browser receives keys normally (Cmd-L, Cmd-W, devtools shortcuts,
etc). The toggle is purely client-side — no device-side release flush
on toggle-off, since the device only knows about the keys we've
sent. Preference persisted in localStorage.

serve-web: help modal triggered by '?'

Modal lists the Ctrl-hotkeys and a brief explainer of how the
keyboard-capture toggle and rotation buttons interact. Opens via the
'?' key or the new util-tray '?' button; closes on Esc, click outside
the card, or the X. While open all keystrokes are gated from the
device so typing into the page (e.g. searching for help) doesn't
leak through.

serve-web: reset _kb_service_id on stream restart

The virtual keyboard surface is host-registered against the live
media stream via UniversalHIDServiceService.create_keyboard_service.
When the stall watchdog restarts the stream, dtuhidd publishes fresh
HID surfaces and the previous _ServiceID becomes stale — every
report posted to it is silently dropped by backboardd.

_stop_hid already drops the UHS/Indigo channel handles; also drop
_kb_service_id so the next /key triggers _ensure_keyboard to
register a fresh surface against the new stream context.

serve-web: collapsible side trays + offline overlay + screenshot/reload

Moves the utility buttons (Sound / Style / Frame / Restart / Help /
Rotate / Keyboard) into a left-side panel that participates in the
document flow instead of position:fixed, so a wide / rotated canvas
can't slide underneath them. Each tray has a chevron toggle to
collapse to a thin strip and reclaim canvas room; the open/closed
state persists in localStorage.

Also lands:
- 'Screenshot' button + Ctrl+P hotkey -> canvas.toBlob saved as PNG
  (uses the canvas backing store as-is so the file matches what the
  user sees, including in-canvas rotation).
- 'Reload' button -> location.reload() for a full client reset
  distinct from /restart (which only restarts the device stream).
- Offline overlay over the canvas when frameCount hasn't advanced
  in ~3 s while subscribed -- gives the user a clear 'stream is

the previous hard-coded 160 px reserve, so collapse/uncollapse
immediately reflows the canvas to the new available space.

serve-web: accessibility settings sidebar

Right-side collapsible tray that mirrors 'pymobiledevice3 developer
accessibility settings show' -- each AXAuditDeviceSetting renders as
a checkbox (bool) or 0..1 slider (float, e.g. DYNAMIC_TYPE), and
edits round-trip through AccessibilityAudit.set_setting on the
device. 'Reset all' calls reset_settings.

Lockdown / DTX comes up lazily on the first /accessibility request,
so a serve-web run that never opens the panel doesn't pay the
usbmuxd handshake cost.

serve-web: close AccessibilityAudit on shutdown

The accessibility sidebar leaked one fresh AccessibilityAudit per
request -- each held an open DTX channel whose reader loop got
cancelled at process exit, producing a stack of 'Channel reader
loop cancelled' ERROR-level tracebacks in the log.

Cache the audit handle on the server, reuse it across panel
interactions, and close it in the shutdown sequence so the DTX
channel exits via the normal close() path (channel._closed=True
suppresses the cancellation traceback). serve-web shutdown is
now clean: one 'shutting down…' line, 'hid worker cancelled'
acknowledgement, 'shutdown complete'.

serve-web: smooth device-rotation animation

Rotation used to snap instantly -- the canvas dim swap + content
redraw all happened in one frame. Add a 300 ms eased CSS transform
on #device-frame so the visual rotation animates while the
canvas-internal rotation still snaps to the final orientation
underneath.

Mechanism: on each setVisualRotation() the canvas dims + content
update immediately (so the surrounding layout reflows now), then
#device-frame gets transform=rotate(-delta) with transition=none
so its visual position matches where it was a moment ago; a
double-RAF then enables a cubic-bezier transition and animates
the transform back to identity. The result is the canvas content
appearing to rotate smoothly into place over 300 ms while the
flex layout reflows in step.

serve-web: drain in-flight /accessibility before closing audit

Hitting /accessibility right before SIGINT produced a 'coroutine
ignored GeneratorExit' RuntimeError on Python 3.14: the request
handler was mid-bplist decode (synchronous plistlib code, not at
an await point) when shutdown closed the audit out from under it,
and the loop's coroutine cleanup couldn't unwind through the
non-awaiting frame.

_stop_accessibility now takes _accessibility_lock first, so any
in-flight handler completes its decode (or hits the outer 3s
shutdown bound) before we tear the DTX channel down. Verified
across 5 stress trials: 0 channel-reader tracebacks, 0 GeneratorExit
warnings, same clean three-line shutdown log.

Feature/core device orientation

serve-web: prevent iOS auto-lock from wedging the stream

Device-side syslog (captured via `pymobiledevice3 syslog live`) showed
the failure mode: when iOS's idle timer dims the display, the
CoreDevice host de-registers its listeners --

  SpringBoard ... ActiveOn->Dimmed: "idle timer"(Idle)
  remoted ERROR: No listener for "com.apple.coredevice.displayservice"
  remoted ERROR: No listener for "com.apple.coredevice.screencaptureservice"

-- so svc.connect() and svc.stop_media_stream() hang on the RemoteXPC
response. The stall watchdog tried to recover by restarting the stream
but the cleanup path took _stream_lock and never released it, leaving
/codec and /stream.bin replying 503 forever.

Three changes:

1. Hold a PreventUserIdleSystemSleep IOPMAssertion via assertion_agent
   for the lifetime of serve(); renew every 2 minutes well under the
   5-minute timeout. This is the actual root-cause fix -- the device
   stops idle-locking, so the listeners stay registered.

2. Bound every device-side RPC in _stop_active_stream / _stop_audio_stream
   with asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=2.0). The shutdown path already

remote: optional no-root iOS 17+ RSD tunnel via a pure-Python userspace stack

Add userspace_tunnel: an in-process, root-free iOS 17+ RSD tunnel built on the
pmd-pytcp userspace stack. UserspaceTun is a TunTapDevice-compatible L2 bridge;
UserspaceDialPlane relays device-bound asyncio.open_connection through it;
establish_userspace_rsd() brings the tunnel up and connects RSD. Provider
selection mirrors `remote start-tunnel` but restricted to root-free paths:
CoreDeviceTunnelProxy on iOS 17.4+, falling back to RemotePairing over bonjour on
17.0-17.3 / Wi-Fi. Resources are owned by a single AsyncExitStack. Wire it into
the CLI via the opt-in --userspace / PYMOBILEDEVICE3_USERSPACE flag, which falls
back to tunneld if pmd-pytcp is absent or establishment fails.

Co-authored-by: renegadelink <30816473+renegadelink@users.noreply.github.com>

remote: drain the kernel tun via add_reader to cut tunneld relay latency

tun_read_task read one packet per asyncio.to_thread hop. Under tunneld's
event loop — shared with the HTTP server and the usb/wifi/usbmux/mobdev2
monitors — each packet's thread-pool result callback queues behind other
loop work, so host->device throughput collapses (AFC push ~2.6 MB/s) even
though the device ingests the data near-instantly and start-tunnel's idle
loop reaches link speed (~37 MB/s).

Read the kernel tun through loop.add_reader instead of a per-packet
to_thread: the fd stays blocking (the reverse self.tun.write path shares
it) and select(timeout=0) drains every buffered packet per readable
callback. The consumer then drains its queue with get_nowait so a busy
loop processes a whole backlog per wakeup rather than yielding per packet.
The userspace tun (no pollable fd) keeps the existing thread-read path;
Windows keeps async_read.

Measured ~2.2x on tunneld AFC upload (2.6 -> 5.6 MB/s), md5-verified both
directions; start-tunnel unchanged at link speed.

remote: serve device-initiated AV (display serve-web) over the userspace tunnel

The screen-mirror media streams are device-initiated UDP: the host binds a UDP
receiver and tells the device to push RTP to it. Over the userspace tunnel that
receiver was a host kernel socket, which the device cannot reach — start_*_stream
failed with "Invalid localIP" and serve-web only worked on the kernel tunnel.

Terminate the RTP on the pytcp stack instead. Add userspace_tunnel.UserspaceUdp:
a UDP socket bound on the stack address, drained by a dedicated reader thread into
an asyncio queue (so the hot receive path is not a per-packet asyncio.to_thread
hop). screen_stream now drives its video and audio receive/RTCP loops through a
small UdpMediaTransport interface with two implementations — _KernelUdp (the
default kernel-tunnel path) and UserspaceUdp — selected by _open_media_receiver,
which also advertises the right address to the device (the stack address in
userspace mode, the RSD connection's local address otherwise).

Verified on an iOS device: `display serve-web --userspace` brings up both audio
and video with no root and streams H.265 end-to-end through /stream.bin.

(`start-server` prints `connect://[<addr>]:<port>`; `lldb` feeds the same to a
spawned lldb). Over the userspace tunnel that address lives only on this process's
in-process PyTCP stack, so an external lldb cannot route to it — the printed steps
were misleading.

Add RemoteServiceDiscoveryService.is_in_process_tunnel (true when the RSD reaches
the device through an injected in-process dialer) and a RoutableTunnelRequiredError.
`debugserver lldb` now fails fast before any build/install; `debugserver start-server`
refuses the remote-address print but still allows --local-port (which forwards via a
localhost listener through the RSD dialer and works over userspace). The error is
surfaced cleanly in __main__ with guidance to use --local-port or a root tunnel.

syslog: parse procid, thread id, image UUIDs and mach timestamp

parse_syslog_entry skipped most of the fixed 129-byte os_trace_relay
entry header. Five more fields live there at stable offsets, verified
against a live iOS 27 device and the os_activity_stream entry encoder in
libsystem_trace:

- procid          (u64 @13)  - per-process; equals pid in practice on iOS
- thread_id       (u64 @83)  - the emitting thread (`thread` stream field)

sending binary. Exposed in `syslog live --format json`.

userspace_tunnel: fix relay teardown hanging the event loop (#1756)

Closing a UserspaceRsdTunnel could hang aclose() and later wedge the
event loop's own shutdown, while leaking one parked rx_pump thread per
relayed connection (the reporter's py-spy dump showed 120 of them).

Three intertwined causes, all in the dial-plane relay:

* A relay handler never finished on its own: the client's EOF was not
  propagated to the device, so rx_pump stayed parked in the PyTCP
  recv() (which does not unblock on close()) and the handler waited on
  device traffic forever. Since Python 3.12.1, Server.wait_closed()
  waits for in-flight connection handlers, so UserspaceDialPlane's
  __aexit__ hung until the caller's timeout.

* The leftover handler tasks were then cancelled at event-loop close
  (e.g. by pytest-asyncio), running psock.close() inline on the loop
  thread — which blocks on the session FSM lock while the (already
  stopped) stack can no longer make progress. The loop wedged for good.

* rx_pump used an untimed blocking recv(), so every relayed connection
  leaked a daemon thread parked in recv() for the process lifetime.

Fixes:

* client_to_device propagates the client's EOF as a half-close
  (shutdown(SHUT_WR)), letting the device answer with its FIN, which
  unblocks rx_pump with EOF and lets the handler complete unaided;
  device_to_client mirrors this with write_eof() toward the client.

* UserspaceDialPlane tracks its in-flight relay tasks and cancels them
  on __aexit__ before wait_closed(), so teardown is prompt and no
  orphan task is left for the loop's shutdown to trip over.

* The handler's psock cleanup (shutdown(SHUT_RDWR) + close()) runs in a
  fire-and-forget daemon thread, never on the event loop, and also
  wakes a recv()-parked rx_pump with EOF.

* rx_pump polls recv() with a timeout and re-checks a closing flag, so
  the thread always exits shortly after teardown.

fix(serve-web): report RCTL OWRD on the RTP media clock to stop phantom-congestion throttle

The RCTL feedback's w4 arrival clock used elapsed-since-start milliseconds
-- a different epoch from the 24kHz RTP media clock the device compares it
against -- so the device computed a bogus 14-50ms OWRD on what is really a
~1ms kernel tunnel, read it as congestion, and throttled framerate (Tx

fix(serve-web): keep the audio RTCP RR flowing during silence

The audio RR keepalive was gated on having already received an audio packet
(_audio_rtp_packets_received != 0). But the screen usually starts silent, so
no audio RTP arrives for a while and the device reaps the audio session at
~20s (RTCPTimeoutInterval) before any audio is ever played -- after which
/audio.bin stays dead. The audio SSRCs are known from negotiation, so send a
valid highest-seq=0 RR from the start to hold the session open through the
silence (video never hit this -- the screen always emits video immediately).

Note: this fixes the reap, but does not by itself restore audible audio on the
iOS-27-beta test unit -- the device streams a constant AAC-ELD silence frame
(payload 00683400) even during Voice Memos playback, i.e. media audio is not
reaching the device's audioSystemOutput capture. That is device-side (or the
test recordings are silent) and separate from this keepalive fix.

fix(serve-vnc): send periodic video RR so the device doesn't reap the stream

serve-vnc sent video PLIs but no periodic Receiver Report. The device's video
streamConfig has RTCPTimeoutEnabled (~25s); PLIs don't reset it, so after ~25s
the device reaped the video session and stopped emitting AUs -- and serve-vnc
has no stream-restart, so it froze permanently on the last frame (looked like
'serve-vnc doesn't work' while serve-web on the same device streamed fine).

Port screen_stream.py's RR keepalive: track the extended highest video seq,
build a compound RR+SDES, and send it once/second (not gated on packets, so a
brief no-frame window at bring-up can't let the session lapse).

encoder 54-60fps continuous, framebuffer updating every frame. And it confirms
native VideoToolbox decode is clean under motion (app-switch transition frames
render crisp) where the browser's WebCodecs HEVC decoder tears -- the
long-standing browser-vs-native gap.

serve-vnc: send framebuffer off the event loop to stop RTP receive starvation

The per-frame full-frame RFB Raw update (width*height*4 -- ~14 MB at
1264x2752) was written through the asyncio StreamWriter (write + drain),
which runs the copy and flush ON the event loop. Under motion with a VNC
client attached, that work starved the RTP socket's sock_recv: the kernel's
receive buffer overflowed and dropped incoming media packets, breaking HEVC
references (mosaic/smear) and collapsing the frame rate. Measured: RTP
ingress dropped from ~60 fps to <15 fps the instant a client attached during
motion, and recovered as soon as the client detached.

Send the framebuffer from a thread-pool executor over a dup() of the client
socket instead. send()/select() release the GIL for the duration of the I/O,
so the event loop keeps draining RTP while the frame goes out. dup() shares
the open file description (and O_NONBLOCK) with asyncio's socket, so the send
path must not setblocking() -- it select()s on the non-blocking fd. The
asyncio side only reads (the recv loop); nothing else writes to the client,
so a dedicated send-direction fd is safe (TCP is full-duplex).

DeviceLink.get_free_disk_space answered DLMessageGetFreeDiskSpace with
shutil.disk_usage().free (statvfs), which on APFS excludes purgeable

userspace_tunnel: drop the pytcp delayed-ACK timer to 1 ms

Every DTX/RemoteXPC round-trip over the userspace tunnel stalled for one
full delayed-ACK timer: the device Nagle-holds the tail segment of each
multi-segment response until our stack ACKs the previous one, and
pmd-pytcp's RFC-default timer is 100 ms. Measured on a USB iPhone, the
round-trip latency is exactly (delay + ~7 ms link RTT), linear across
1..100 ms — so 'dvt ls /' paid ~110 ms per operation, and the RSD/DTX
handshakes paid several timers each.

Set 'tcp.delayed_ack.delay_ms' to 1 (effectively ACK-immediately) through
the same registered-knob check as the other throughput sysctls, so an
older pmd-pytcp just logs and runs untuned.

Measured (iPhone12,1, USB):
- dvt ls / round-trip: 110 ms -> 8 ms
- RSD connect: 400 ms -> ~85 ms; DTX connect: 190 ms -> ~78 ms
- full 'dvt ls /' CLI: 1.45 s -> 0.82 s
- bulk transfers unaffected: DSC download 38-39 MB/s at 1/10/100 ms alike
  (streams are paced by the ACK-every-other-segment rule, not the timer)

userspace_tunnel: drain the stack egress in batches and hoist per-packet constants

The userspace branch of tun_read_task paid one event-loop reschedule per
outbound packet ('await async_read()' + per-packet drain) — on the same
loop that runs the whole pytcp stack. The kernel-tun path already
batch-drains for exactly this reason (_tun_read_loop_via_reader); give
the userspace tun the same treatment: async_read_batch() awaits one
frame, then greedily drains every frame already queued on the socketpair,
so one wakeup services a whole egress burst.

tun_read_task now prefers the batch surface on every platform — this also
moves Windows off the per-packet win32 branch, which the userspace tun
used to fall into.

Also hoist the two per-packet constants out of the hot paths: the
Ethernet header prepended to every inbound packet was re-derived (string
parsing + struct packing) on each write(), and the EtherType check
re-unpacked per frame.

healthy. tcp.plpmtud.probe_timer_ms=1500 and tcp.rto.min_ms=200 keep

userspace_tunnel: wait for the stack address before declaring the tun up

The pytcp stack installs the interface address from its own tasks shortly

slack.

lands within a tick or two, bounded at 5s) until the address is present in

dvt: fix silently-dropped process kill over the userspace tunnel

ProcessControl.kill() invoked the fire-and-forget 'killPid:' DTX selector
(expects_reply=False). With no reply there is no round-trip barrier, so the
CLI's 'async with' tore down the DTX channel — and, on iOS 17+, the tunnel —
before the device acted on the message, and the kill was silently dropped:
the target process kept running. This surfaced once the no-root userspace
tunnel became the default (its teardown races in-flight data more tightly
than the privileged kernel tunnel did); 'developer dvt kill <pid>' no-oped on
iOS 27 while 'developer dvt signal <pid> -s KILL' worked.

Implement kill() via 'sendSignal:toPid:' with SIGKILL instead. That selector
awaits a reply, and the round-trip guarantees the device has processed the
request before teardown. Verified live on an iOS 27 device: SpringBoard is
now reliably terminated and respawns under a fresh pid. The device-only
test_kill now asserts the pid changed so a dropped kill can no longer pass
vacuously.

irecv: dispose the USB handle in _reinit to fix restore hang after reset

Fixes a regression introduced in v9.40.0 where a device restore hangs at
"If the restore hangs here, disconnect & reconnect the device": _find() spins
forever and never re-acquires the device after reset() ("no device in the
desired mode"), while a fresh re-run of the restore succeeds.

Root cause: v9.40.0's typing cleanup introduced local captures like
`device = self.device` in send_buffer(). send_buffer() calls self.reset() ->
_reinit() while that local is still live, so setting `self._device = None` no
longer drops the last reference — the usb.core.Device is not garbage-collected
and its libusb handle stays claimed. The reset device then can't re-enumerate
cleanly and the subsequent _find() reads a stale device / loops.

_reinit() now calls usb.util.dispose_resources() on the outgoing device before
dropping it, releasing the handle explicitly instead of relying on refcount/GC.

webinspector: modern Chrome DevTools debugging over CDP

Run the CDP server on the CLI event loop and translate WebKit's Web Inspector
protocol to the Chrome DevTools Protocol so a modern Chrome DevTools frontend
can inspect iOS WebViews: /json discovery, a per-page WebSocket, the
Runtime/Debugger/Page/DOM/Network/CSS domains the frontend drives on startup,
and a screencast of the device screen. Includes end-to-end tests exercised
against a real device.

webinspector: keep the CDP bridge alive under process swaps and stalls

WebKit swaps the WebContent process on cross-site navigation and can leave a
target unresponsive, which naively stalls or kills the whole session. Survive
process swaps by replaying the frontend's domain setup onto the new target;
bound every device round-trip so a wedged target backs off - and self-heals as
soon as it answers again - instead of freezing the bridge; and abandon a wait
as soon as its target is destroyed. Includes tests.

webinspector: robust CDP screencast

Keep the device-screen stream alive through transient hiccups: don't freeze on
a dropped/absent snapshot frame, allocate a unique message id per frame so a
delayed response can't be mismatched to a later request, throttle synthesized
mousemoves, and fire real key events for Enter so the device actually receives
console/URL input. Drop screencast-input synthesis and WebKit-only events that
would otherwise flood the frontend. Includes tests.

webinspector: correct console evaluation and script translation

Make the console usable: return a scriptId from Runtime.compileScript and keep
the handler robust when the device is busy; stop leaking the bridge's own
internal evaluation scripts into Chrome's debugger model; normalize WebKit's
multi-line native-function descriptions to Chrome's single-line form (the
console's argument-hint parser rejects anything else); and never emit a null
url in Page.getNavigationHistory (it crashes the screencast panel and blanks
the inspector).

webinspector: serve the DevTools frontend to bypass chrome://inspect's relay

chrome://inspect inspects a network-discovered target through Chrome's
browser-process relay, which deadlocks under sustained console traffic and
freezes the console and screencast until the window is reloaded - independent
of anything the bridge sends. Serve the DevTools frontend from the bridge
instead: a landing page at / links each page to a direct-connect frontend, and
/devtools/{path} proxies the hosted frontend build over http. Opened as an
ordinary http page it connects to the bridge's WebSocket directly, bypassing
the relay entirely. Point the CLI at http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ instead of
chrome://inspect.

webinspector: fall back to a local Chrome for the DevTools frontend

The DevTools frontend is proxied from the officially hosted build, which
requires network access. When that host is unreachable (offline), launch a
throwaway headless Chrome and proxy its own bundled frontend instead, so the
bridge keeps working without connectivity.

Chrome is located on PATH or in the platform's known install locations;
--chrome <path> overrides discovery. If no Chrome is found and the hosted
build is unreachable, the frontend routes return 404 with a clear log line.

webinspector: make the debugger pause on debugger statements and breakpoints

Two WebKit quirks made the debugger never stop, and Chrome's frontend papers over neither
because its own backend behaves differently:

1. Chrome assumes breakpoints default to ACTIVE and only sends Debugger.setBreakpointsActive
   when the user *deactivates* them - it never sends it on connect. WebKit instead deactivates
   breakpoints on enable, so nothing (breakpoints or `debugger;`) ever paused.
2. Pausing on `debugger;` is separately gated behind Debugger.setPauseOnDebuggerStatements,
   which defaults OFF and has no Chrome equivalent (Chrome pauses on `debugger;` whenever the
   debugger is attached and breakpoints are active).

Establish both on Debugger.enable and keep setPauseOnDebuggerStatements in lockstep with the
frontend's Deactivate-breakpoints toggle; both replay onto fresh targets after a process swap.

Also translate WebKit's Debugger.paused payload to Chrome's schema: fill the per-callFrame
`url` WebKit omits (from Debugger.scriptParsed) and map WebKit-only scope types
(functionName, globalLexicalEnvironment, ...) to valid Chrome Scope.type values - otherwise
Chrome's SDK throws while building the paused state and the Sources panel never shows the pause.

Verified against the exact command sequence a live Chrome sends: `debugger;` statements and
Debugger.setBreakpointByUrl breakpoints both pause, with a schema-valid paused payload.

webinspector: stop console eager-evaluation from running side effects

Chrome's console previews the current line as you type by evaluating it with
throwOnSideEffect=true, relying on V8 to abort the instant the expression would
cause a side effect - so typing `console.log(4234)` shows no preview and does
NOT log until Enter. WebKit's Runtime.evaluate has no such guard, so the bridge
forwarded the preview and WebKit ran it for real: the console logged (and any
other side effect fired) on every keystroke.

Intercept eager-evaluation Runtime.evaluate (throwOnSideEffect set) and answer
it the way V8 does for a side-effecting expression - a side-effect error, so
DevTools shows no preview and nothing executes. The real evaluation on Enter
carries no throwOnSideEffect and is forwarded unchanged.

Autocomplete uses the same throwOnSideEffect evaluate on sub-expressions (the
completion list's base object, the argument hint's callee) under a dedicated
objectGroup; those are side-effect-free lookups the dropdown needs, so they are
forwarded rather than refused - otherwise autocomplete would break.

Verified by driving a real Chrome DevTools console against the bridge: typing
`console.log(<n>)` no longer logs before Enter, while completion and argument
hints still work.

tests: Fix ssl_start_sync failure test on Python <= 3.10

test_ssl_start_sync_failure_raises_connection_terminated fails on 3.9 and 3.10
while passing on 3.11+. The error is a ResourceWarning escalated by pytest's
unraisable-exception plugin:

    PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning: Exception ignored in:
    <ssl.SSLSocket fd=11, family=AddressFamily.AF_UNIX, ...>

On those versions CPython leaves the half-built SSLSocket unclosed when the
handshake fails inside wrap_socket(). It is not a pymobiledevice3 bug -- the same
ResourceWarning reproduces with plain CPython and no library code:

    c, s = socket.socketpair(); s.close()
    ctx.wrap_socket(c)   # -> ResourceWarning: unclosed <ssl.SSLSocket fd=3, ...>

The socket is never ours to close: wrap_socket() creates and owns it, and
ssl_start_sync deliberately does not touch the original afterwards (which is what
the test asserts). So the fix belongs in the test, not the error path.

Not caught by CI because the workflow runs `pytest -m cli`, which deselects this
file on every matrix version.

remotexpc: Add outbound XPC file transfer support

The transport could receive file transfers but not send them, which blocks every
service that uploads (cryptexd install, installcoordination's AssetStreamFD).

Four wire rules, each established from device syslog (subsystem com.apple.xpc.remote):

- The stream must be odd. HEADERS on an even stream is answered with
  GOAWAY error 1 "request HEADERS: invalid stream_id"; even streams are
  server-initiated, and the receive path only uses them because the device
  created them first.
- The opening preamble must carry the transfer id as the XPC message_id, else
  the device logs "Got HEADER with invalid msg_id 0" and drops the connection.
  With it set it logs "Found pending stream ID for <id>".
- The payload follows the preamble immediately. The FILE_TX_STREAM_RESPONSE
  preamble is an acknowledgement that arrives after the data, not a gate;
  waiting for it makes the device reset the stream (RST_STREAM error 5).
- The device resets a transfer stream once it has the payload. That is normal
  completion, so finished streams are tracked and their resets ignored.

Outbound flow control had to be added with it: incoming WINDOW_UPDATE frames were
discarded, and the peer grants its connection window during the handshake, so
missing it caps transfers at the 65535 default. The preamble is itself a DATA
frame and must be charged against the window too -- not doing so overruns it once
a previous transfer has drained it and earns GOAWAY error 3.

Verified against an iPhone on iOS 27: a 15.9MB image plus four smaller payloads
delivered in one request, consumed by cryptexd at the exact announced sizes.

darwin_errno: Add device-side errno table

Several device services report failures as a raw errno produced by the device,
which runs Darwin. Rendering those with os.strerror or the stdlib errno module
resolves them against the host's C runtime, so a Windows or Linux host prints the
wrong name for the same number -- the numbering diverges above ~34, and
ENOTCAPABLE (107) does not exist on Linux at all.

The table is generated from Darwin's sys/errno.h so it is correct regardless of
host. Kept out of osu/posix_util.py deliberately: that is a host-OS abstraction
swapped for win_util on Windows, which is exactly the platform this needs to work
on.

lockdown notification proxy the repo tunnels through its .shim.remote alias. The
message vocabulary is identical (PostNotification / ObserveNotification /
RelayNotification); only the transport differs.

Exposed as --remotexpc on the existing notification commands, which keeps one
place to look and names the transport rather than implying one form is more

apps: Add install-record via installcoordination_proxy

com.apple.remote.installcoordination_proxy exposes the LaunchServices install
record for an application (DB UUID/sequence, install path, persistent identifier).

Two properties of this service are unusual and worth stating, since both cause a
silent hang otherwise:

- Every request must carry RequestVersion and ProtocolVersion. If either is
  missing the daemon cancels the connection without replying at all.
- Replies arrive as fresh messages on the connection rather than XPC replies, so
  the client reads from the stream instead of awaiting a reply id.

The daemon is the same binary on macOS, where handlers are TARGET_OS_OSX-gated to
require Path and reject BundleID. iOS is the opposite -- confirmed on device:
BundleID works, Path returns an error.

Only the read-only Query request is implemented. Install additionally streams its
payload over an out-of-band file transfer.

tss: Add Cryptex1 personalization request

add_ap_tags skips every Cryptex1,* key because AP tickets do not carry them, which
left no way to build a cryptex request at all. add_cryptex1_tags emits the other
shape: @Cryptex1,Ticket, the Cryptex1 chip parameters, and digests for only the
personalized components.

Both details come from decoding a ticket Xcode obtained for this device:

- Cryptex1,GenericDmg is declared Personalize: False and is absent from the signed
  manifest, which carries digests for ginf/gtcd/gtgv only.
- The nonce is signed raw, not hashed -- the ticket's cnch tag matches the value
  get-nonce returns byte for byte.

Also records the CoreDevice signing-server override (ddiSigningServer) next to the
existing AuthInstallSigningServerURL note.

Not working end to end: Apple rejects the request as built here (@Cryptex1,Ticket

cryptex: Add cryptexd service and CLI group

com.apple.security.cryptexd.remote manages cryptexes -- including the personalized
DeveloperDiskImage, which iOS 17+ installs as one. The wire format is
{"routine": ..., "argv": {...}} answered with {"error": 0, "argv": ...} or a
cferr, where error is a device-side Darwin errno.

Its own group rather than a subcommand of mounter: every command needs an RSD
tunnel while mounter works over USB, the mounter is a consumer of the cryptex
subsystem rather than its parent, and nesting forced a cryptex- prefix onto every
command name.

Verified against an iPhone on iOS 27: read-personalization-id, copy-installed,
get-nonce and uninstall, the last against real state. copy-installed reports a
mounted DDI as com.apple.MobileAsset.DDI, which nothing else in the repo surfaces.

Two caveats are documented in the code:

- roll-nonce does not work. No argv shape found so far actually rolls the nonce;
  in argv the daemon reports the key missing, at top level it replies without
  error and leaves the nonce unchanged.
- install sends the request Xcode sends, captured off the wire from a devicectl
  install, and the daemon accepts it and consumes all five payloads. It cannot
  complete until add_cryptex1_tags can produce a ticket Apple will sign.

tss: Fix the Cryptex1 personalization request

Apple rejected every Cryptex1 request with a bare "An internal error occurred."
The shape was wrong in three ways, all of them visible by comparing against
what Xcode sends -- CoreDeviceService logs the dictionary it is about to sign
under the `com.apple.libcryptex:scrivener` subsystem, so a `devicectl` DDI
install can be read straight out of the unified log:

    log show --last 5m --info --debug --predicate 'process == "CoreDeviceService"'

A Cryptex1 request identifies the device solely by `Cryptex1,UDID` (the chip ID
and ECID concatenated big-endian); the six `Ap*` tags an AP request carries must
not appear. Each personalized component contributes nothing but its `Digest` --
no `EPRO`/`ESEC`/`Trusted` decoration from RestoreRequestRules. And
`Cryptex1,ProductionMode` and `Cryptex1,UniqueTagList` were missing entirely.

The resulting ticket decodes identically to Xcode's, tag for tag, except for
`srvn` -- the nonce TSS generates per request.

cryptex: Personalize against the nonce domain's handle, not its index

`auto_install_ddi` read the cryptex nonce with `get_nonce(nonce_domain=...)`,
passing a build identity's `Cryptex1,NonceDomain`. That value is a nonce domain
*handle*, and the daemon's handle and index tables disagree: on an iPhone 11 the
DDI cryptex is handle 4 == index 10, while index 4 is an unrelated domain.

The ticket therefore committed to the wrong nonce, and the device rejected it
while importing the first asset -- reported as `invalid asset: ginf`, and
narrated in the device's own log as
`Manifest no longer valid [70: Stale NFS file handle]`.

Also guard `auto_install_ddi` with `AlreadyMountedError` when the DDI cryptex is
already installed, instead of spending a TSS round-trip to have cryptexd answer
EEXIST.

cryptex: Add `auto-install`, downloading and caching the DDI

Installs the DeveloperDiskImage as a cryptex through `cryptexd` alone, without
the image mounter -- the cryptex counterpart of `mounter auto-mount`, named for
the fact that a cryptex is installed rather than mounted. The end result is
indistinguishable: `mounter list` reports it as a `Personalized` image at
`/System/Developer`.

The Cryptex1 assets used to exist only inside Xcode's bundle, which limited this
to macOS hosts with Xcode installed. They are now published by the
DeveloperDiskImage repository, so `fetch_cryptex_ddi` downloads and caches them
under the home folder exactly as `fetch_personalized_ddi` does, and
`--restore-dir` stays available for a local bundle. Each payload is written to
the path the downloaded build manifest declares for it, which makes the cache a
`Restore` directory `load_cryptex1_assets` reads back directly.

Bump `LATEST_DDI_BUILD_ID` to 27A5228h to match what the repository publishes,
and check it on the cryptex path too, so a stale bundle warns up front instead
of failing obscurely during import.

`com.apple.libcryptex:scrivener`, which is the only workable route -- the
`ddiSigningServer` plaintext redirect yields nothing because CoreDevice reuses a
cached ticket, and gs.apple.com is pinned against MITM.

Offer `cryptex auto-install` alongside `mounter auto-mount` where readers look

described this correctly; AGENTS.md was the outlier, and reading it is what put

device_link: Make discarded-file bookkeeping O(1) for non-directories

Every payload rejected by a backup filter leaves a placeholder tracked in
_discarded_files, and the device's finalize issues one move per sent
file. _discarded_files_below scanned the whole set (building each
candidate's pathlib parent chain) on every move/copy/remove, so a
filtered whole-device backup went quadratic: at the scale reported in
the issue (~76k moves x ~74.5k placeholders) the finalize projects to
~3 hours of CPU pegged at ~97% progress.

The set only ever contains file paths, so unless the operated-on path is
a directory the only possible match is the path itself — an O(1)
membership test. Thread that knowledge from the callers, which already
know it (move: the destination mirrors the moved kind; copy/remove:
is_dir was already computed); only genuine directory operations still
scan. The same benchmark now finishes the whole move phase in 0.35s.

userspace-tunnel: fully close abandoned relay sockets; consume pmd-pytcp 0.3.4

The relay handler propagated a client's EOF to the device as a
half-close (shutdown(SHUT_WR)) and kept reading. That protected a
half-close pattern nothing uses — every ServiceConnection teardown
in pymobiledevice3 is a full close — and it kept the pytcp socket
open, so the session was never ORPHANED and pmd-pytcp's FIN_WAIT_2
reaper (deliberately orphan-only, Linux tcp_fin_timeout parity)
never armed. Against a device that neither sent a byte nor FINed
the connection, the handler parked at psock.recv() forever.
Measured live on a USB iPhone (iOS 27.0): 24 of 30 abandoned
service connections leaked their handler task, pytcp socket, and
session until tunnel teardown; long-lived sessions (the CLI keeps
its tunnel for the process lifetime) accumulated them without
bound.

Client EOF now fully closes the pytcp socket: the FIN still goes
out — services that treat EOF as "finish and close" behave exactly
as before — but a silent device leaves an orphan the reaper frees,
and with pmd-pytcp >= 0.3.4 the session's death wakes the parked
recv() so the handler finishes promptly. Re-measured: 0 of 30
abandoned connections leave anything behind.

The pmd-pytcp floor moves to 0.3.4, which ships the other half of
this fix plus the audit's tunnel-killers: session death (RST / FIN
/ reaper / 2MSL) wakes blocked receivers and surfaces RST as
ConnectionResetError; NUD FAILED restarts resolution on TX (a
device asleep ~3 s could previously black-hole the tunnel until
process restart); CLOSING gets an exit guarantee; datagram close()
wakes blocked receivers (UserspaceUdp readers no longer hang on
close); and gracefully closed sessions stop spinning a 1 kHz timer
through TIME_WAIT.

Also: UserspaceTun.close() clears the stack-init marker in a
finally, so an open->close->open cycle re-runs stack.init() even
when stop() raised.

Tests: the relay conversation test now pins the full-close
completion (no device action required), and a new abandoned-client
/ silent-device regression pins the leak fix; the fake pytcp
socket mirrors 0.3.4's death-wakes-recv semantics. Verified live:
stuck-task census 48 -> 0; throughput and dvt-ls latency unchanged
(0.79-0.82 s vs 0.80-0.81 s baseline).

cli: adopt PEP 810 lazy imports on Python 3.15+ (no-op on older versions)

Importing pymobiledevice3._lazy_imports flips the process to lazy-imports
mode, filtered so only imports performed by pymobiledevice3's own modules
become lazy -- third-party packages' internals stay eager (unscoped
process-wide laziness is known to break import hooks, e.g. pytest's
assertion rewriter trips over a lazy fnmatch proxy).

The CLI entry (__main__) and tests/conftest.py import it first in their
first-party block; on Python <= 3.14 it is a no-op, keeping the 3.9 floor.

Measured on 3.15.0b3 (macOS arm64, warm cache, device connected):
- pymobiledevice3 --help: 0.55s -> 0.23s
- pymobiledevice3 usbmux list: 0.53s -> 0.39s (rest is device I/O)
- full test suite against a physical device: identical results lazy vs eager

device_link: chunk download_files at 32 KiB to avoid BackupAgent2 OOM

On an incremental backup the host sends the previous Manifest.db back to the
device (DLMessageDownloadFiles) so BackupAgent2 can diff it. BackupAgent2
buffers a whole protocol frame in memory before flushing to disk, so the old
128 MiB frame size drives its RSS up; a large Manifest.db (~1.5 GB) pushes it
past its jetsam memory limit and the process is killed mid-transfer, leaving the
backup hung at 0% (issues #1165, #1857).

Apple's own DeviceLink.framework (the host side Finder uses) sends file data in
32 KiB frames by default -- the "BufferSize" preference under com.apple.DeviceLink;
_DLSendFileForBulkOperation reads BufferSize-1 bytes per frame. Match that.

Measured against a 1.55 GB Manifest.db sent to an incremental backup: 128 MiB
frames breach the device memory limit and crawl at ~8.5 MB/s, while 32 KiB frames
stay under it and complete ~4.6x faster (~40 MB/s, same as 1 MiB). The prior note
that "even 32 KiB chunks did not help" (#1165) referred to the old code that
declared a single whole-file frame and only split the socket writes; with correct
per-frame framing the frame size is what bounds the device's memory use.

feat(afc): mount AFC filesystems in Finder over WebDAV

Add a `webdav` subcommand to each AFC-backed CLI group that serves the
device's AFC filesystem over a local async WebDAV server (ASGIWebDAV) so a
WebDAV client (macOS Finder, Windows Explorer, GNOME Files, ...) can browse
and edit it read-write as a mounted volume:

- pymobiledevice3 afc webdav [PATH] [--mount]
- pymobiledevice3 apps webdav BUNDLE_ID [PATH] [--documents] [--mount]
- pymobiledevice3 crash webdav [PATH] [--mount]

Each request is translated into AfcService calls; AFC's response demuxing
makes concurrent requests over one connection safe. `--mount` mounts and
reveals the volume using the host's native mechanism (mount_webdav on macOS,
net use on Windows, gio on Linux), falling back to printing the URL when none
is available; the mount point is named pmd-<udid>-<service>-<rand> so it is
easy to spot in Finder.

The provider swallows Finder metadata writes (.DS_Store / AppleDouble ._*),
refuses to open non-regular files, and translates AFC errors into clean
WebDAV statuses.

ASGIWebDAV requires Python >= 3.10; the dependency is gated accordingly
(with backports.zstd on 3.10-3.13) and the CLI surfaces a clear message on
3.9. httpx is added to the test extra.

usbmux: don't flip the returned socket back to blocking mode

MuxConnection.connect() set the socket to blocking right before handing
it to the caller — a leftover from the sync API contract, carried over
in the asyncio migration. Every consumer drives the socket via asyncio:
ServiceConnection.__init__ immediately flips it back to non-blocking,
and the WDA reachability probe discards it. A blocking socket passed to
loop.sock_recv() would stall the entire event loop (or raise in asyncio
debug mode), so return it non-blocking, matching the async contract.

dtx: Register NSKeyedArchive classes explicitly for lazy imports

The DTX NSKeyedArchive proxy classes (DTSysmonTapMessage,
DTTapHeartbeatMessage, ...) were registered with bpylist2 only as an
import-time side effect of pymobiledevice3.dtx.ns_types. Under PEP 810

names is used, so decode paths that reach archiver.unarchive() without
touching an ns_types name (e.g. `sysmon`) saw an unpopulated class map
and fell back to plistlib, logging a decode warning per message.

register_ns_keyed_classes() and call it from the modules owning the
unarchive call sites (message.py, message_aux.py) instead of relying on
a bare side-effect import.

XCTest result types are decoded by the DTX machinery without any
xctest_types name being touched, so under PEP 810 lazy imports
