webdav: Close the server when the device disconnects

Previously the WebDAV runner blocked on a fresh asyncio.Event that nothing
ever set, so when the device disconnected the server, the local mount, and
the process all stayed open serving errors until Ctrl-C.

AfcService now exposes wait_terminated(): a sticky event set whenever the
background reader loop exits (the task handle itself is not a stable signal
since _send_and_wait restarts exited readers). The WebDAV runner waits on
it, tears down (unmount, stop), and raises ConnectionTerminatedError so the
CLI's global --reconnect machinery can wait for the device and re-serve.
Ctrl-C behavior is unchanged.

Verified end-to-end against a physical device: rebooting the device while
serving prints 'Device disconnected; stopping.' and exits within seconds.

cli: Make --reconnect wait for and re-target the originally selected device

The --reconnect retry loop waited for *any* device and re-invoked the
command from scratch, which misbehaved with multiple devices attached:
another device satisfied the wait instantly, the re-invocation failed with
DeviceNotFoundError (not treated as reconnectable, killing the loop), and
a device chosen at the interactive prompt was forgotten entirely -- the
re-invocation silently auto-picked another attached device while the
target was still rebooting.

The service-provider dependencies now record which device they resolved to
(explicit --udid, auto-pick, or prompt). The reconnect loop waits for that
specific device, treats DeviceNotFoundError as reconnectable, and stamps
PYMOBILEDEVICE3_UDID before re-invoking so the same device is
deterministically re-targeted without a second prompt.

Verified end-to-end through a pty with two devices attached: selecting the
second device at the prompt, then rebooting it, re-serves that same device
(proven by a marker file only it has) with no second prompt.

The main()-invoking tests run coroutines on a private loop: asyncio.run's
cleanup unsets the main-thread event loop, which on Python 3.9 breaks later
sync tests that construct loop-binding asyncio primitives.

webdav: serve Range requests to prevent large-file corruption (#1866)

AfcDavProvider declared content_range=False and ignored the HTTP Range header,
answering every GET with 200 and the entire file body. macOS Finder / webdavfs
reads large files as a series of byte ranges; receiving the whole file in
response to `Range: bytes=X-Y` makes the client write the full body at offset X,
producing a corrupted file.

Honor Range requests like asgi_webdav's own FileSystemProvider: advertise
Accept-Ranges, return 206 Partial Content with a body generator that seeks to
the requested offset and streams only the requested bytes (with 416 handling for
a failed If-Range).

This needs seeking within an open AFC handle, so add AfcService.fseek() using
the existing FILE_SEEK opcode.

userspace-tunnel: right-size the tun socketpair buffers to 6 MiB

The datagram socketpair buffers exist to absorb a burst of one full
receive window of packets (tcp.rcv_wnd_max = 4 MiB); 8 MiB was double
that for no measurable benefit. 6 MiB keeps 1.5x headroom over the
window and measures identically on a real device: a DSC fetch over the

userspace-tunnel: relay dialed connections over unix domain sockets

The dial plane's relays listened on loopback TCP: an unauthenticated
port through which any local process could reach the device's RSD/DVT/
lockdown services for the tunnel's whole lifetime. Bind them to unix
sockets in a 0700 temp directory instead, so filesystem permissions
decide who may connect; loopback TCP remains the fallback where AF_UNIX
is unavailable (per the new OsUtils.supports_unix_sockets, e.g. on
Windows). The socket directory is removed on dial-plane exit.
AFC-over-tunnel throughput is unchanged (measured at parity in both
directions).

Fixes surfaced by the switch, all reachable on the TCP fallback too:

- create_using_tcp: skip keep-alive for relay-leg connections — an
  injected open_connection dialer means a process-local relay leg (the
  fact is_in_process_tunnel is defined by), where keep-alive is at best
  pointless loopback chatter and raises OSError on a unix socket. Also
  close the writer on any setup failure instead of leaking the
  established connection.
- dial plane: a dial's connect completes in the kernel before the accept
  callback spawns the relay handler, so a handler could register after
  __aexit__ snapshot-cancelled _relay_tasks and park forever, hanging
  Server.wait_closed(). Drain the queued accepts with a _closing gate,
  keep cancelling until no handlers remain, and close the accepted
  transport when a handler is cancelled mid-connect.

Verified live against an iOS device (RSD + lockdown + AFC over the
relays).

userspace-tunnel: env var to force loopback-TCP relays

PYMOBILEDEVICE3_USERSPACE_TCP_RELAY (any non-empty value) makes the dial
plane bind its relays on loopback TCP even where AF_UNIX exists,
reproducing the Windows relay path on any platform for debugging. As a
side effect the new test gives the TCP relay path POSIX CI coverage (it
was otherwise exercised only on Windows runners).

Verified live against a device (full tunnel over forced-TCP relays).

userspace-tunnel: tear down when the tunnel transport dies

When the outer transport dies — e.g. the USB cable is pulled and
usbmuxd closes the CoreDeviceProxy connection — the transport read task
just ended and nothing woke the pytcp sessions or the relay handlers:
every in-flight service read parked forever (reproduced live: `dvt
oslog` stuck indefinitely after unplug, on both relay flavors).
Keep-alive cannot cover this path: a relay's peer is this very process,
so loopback probes are always answered regardless of the device
(measured: 15 s of active keep-alive on the TCP relay never fired).
The kernel-tunnel path is unaffected — there the utun interface
disappears and connections error out on their own.

Watch the tunnel client's wait_closed() (it returns exactly when the
read task ends) and tear the whole userspace RSD down: the dial-plane
teardown cancels the relay handlers, surfacing EOF/connection errors to
every blocked caller. Verified live: `dvt oslog` now exits within a
second of the transport dying.

Not folded into the relay commit deliberately: this hole predates it
(the loopback-TCP relays hung identically).

userspace-tunnel: apply review findings

Adversarial review of the relay/teardown work surfaced these; all
verified against a live repro or instrumented trace:

- remotexpc: RemoteXPCConnection.local_address raised IndexError over
  the userspace tunnel (an AF_UNIX sockname is a string, not a tuple).
  Raise a clear error instead: neither the unix path nor the old TCP
  relay's ('127.0.0.1', port) was ever reachable by the device.
- dial plane: a dial racing (or following) teardown re-created the
  socket dir and registered a live relay server after teardown had
  cleared both — leaked until process exit, and the caller got a stream
  that only ever yields EOF. The transport watcher made this window
  practical (teardown now runs concurrently with dials on device
  disconnect). Dials now fail with ConnectionError once closing.
- dial plane: log the unix-socket-bind fallback to loopback TCP at
  warning — it silently traded the socket dir's 0700 access control for
  a port any local process can connect to.
- transport watcher: guard aclose() — it runs fire-and-forget exactly
  when unwinding is most likely to raise (the transport just died), and
  an exception only surfaced as 'Task exception was never retrieved'.
- __aexit__: correct the pre-close tick's comment (it lets a queued
  accept attach to a still-open Server; the gate handler closes the
  transport later, during wait_closed) and drop the cancel re-loop —
  the _closing gate makes registration-after-snapshot impossible.
- tests: use close_stream_writer instead of hand-rolled close (it has
  hang protection), run the unix-socket test under the context manager
  so a failing assertion cannot leak the relay server, and pin the
  dial-after-close ConnectionError.

userspace-tunnel: bind one eager relay listener; route the port in-band

The dial plane bound one listener per device service port, lazily on
the dial path — the listener you connected to was the port routing. A
post-release race hunt (deterministic probes + randomized dial/cancel/
teardown storms on both relay flavors) kept finding leaks in that
shape, each fixable only with another guard:

- a dial parked in the listener bind while teardown swept _servers
  registered a live listener nothing would ever close (wide window on
  the TCP fallback: start_server resolves through the getaddrinfo
  executor; on the unix path the raced bind lands ENOENT after the
  socket-dir removal and falls back to a loopback TCP listener);
- a cancellation landing on create_server's final suspension — routine
  via create_using_tcp's connect timeout — orphaned a serving listener
  the loop's selector keeps alive forever;
- N concurrent first dials to one port each bound their own listener.

Route the port in-band instead: dial() writes a 2-byte header after
connecting and the handler reads it, so ONE listener serves every port
and is bound eagerly in __aenter__ — before any dial exists. Nothing
binds on the dial path anymore, so no bind can race a timeout, a
cancellation, or teardown, and the per-port cache, its lock, and their
guards are structurally unnecessary. The bind-cancellation hazard is
still shielded (_bind_listener) for the one remaining bind site.

Teardown lets in-flight connects land against the still-open listener
before closing it — a connect completing against a just-closed Server
makes asyncio's accept path abandon the accepted socket unclosed — and
a dial landing after teardown began raises ConnectionError instead of
returning a stream that could only yield EOF.

Verified: full probe battery clean on both flavors (zero fd/task
deltas, zero ResourceWarnings with stderr accounted separately); live
device — RSD + lockdown + AFC at benchmark parity, dvt oslog, and 1 s
teardown on transport death.

userspace-tunnel: serialize the singleton lifecycle; shed headerless relay connections

Two hardening fixes from continuing the leak/race hunt:

- Every open/close transition of the process-global pytcp stack now
  serializes on one module-level lifecycle lock (per event loop,
  created inside the loop — Python 3.9 primitives bind their loop at
  construction). Before, two concurrent establish_userspace_rsd()/
  aopen() calls both passed the singleton guard — checked at entry,
  published only after the whole establishment — and drove the one
  stack at once: measured live, every racer failed with
  IncompleteReadError and the stack was left half-started (pmd-pytcp
  asserting 'ARP Cache.start() called while a worker is still
  running'). An explicit aclose() during the transport watcher's unwind
  likewise waits for it instead of returning early, so
  disconnect-then-reopen cannot race the stack's shutdown, and
  establish_userspace_rsd() shares the winner's tunnel when it loses
  the race for the same device (three concurrent callers all get the
  one RSD, verified live).
- A relay connection that never sends its 2-byte port header (on the
  TCP fallback any local process can connect) pinned a handler and its
  accepted transport until tunnel close; it is now shed after
  RELAY_HEADER_TIMEOUT. dial() writes the header before returning, so
  legitimate connections are unaffected.

userspace-tunnel: close the CLI tunnel at exit instead of hard-exiting

force_exit's os._exit existed to skip costs that no longer exist: the
pure-asyncio stack has no threads that could park interpreter exit, the
CLI's persistent loop is abandoned rather than closed (so there is no
pending-task GC noise to mute), and a clean aclose() measures ~3 ms
against a live device. Register a bounded clean close at atexit instead
— the device gets a FIN for its sessions rather than an abandoned
tunnel, exit codes and other libraries' atexit handlers work normally,
and the hard-exit escape hatch is gone.

docs: add 'Understanding the network stacks' guide

Diagrams for all four transport paths — usbmux, Wi-Fi lockdown, kernel
tunnel, and the userspace tunnel (layer stack, dial sequence, disconnect
teardown) — with the properties that fall out of each shape. Enables

userspace-tunnel: don't rely on wait_for for the relay header timeout

On Python <= 3.11, asyncio.wait_for can swallow an external cancellation
that races the awaited future's completion — teardown's cancel of a
handler whose header arrived in the same window was lost, and __aexit__
waited on that handler forever (flaked on slow CI runners; local runs
won the race). Enforce the header timeout with loop.call_later closing
the transport instead — readexactly then fails and the handler sheds —
and repeat teardown's cancel pass a few times as a backstop against any
future cancellation-swallow of the same shape.

docs: explain why the RSD path suspends remoted

The reason start-tunnel/tunneld suspend macOS remoted was never written down,
and was long attributed to the device closing the host's RSD fd during pairing.
Root-caused empirically: the contention is at the direct RSD RemoteXPC connect
(port 58783 over the USB NCM link), where the device resets a second root
channel while remoted owns the link. It is unrelated to pairing (reproduces on
an already-paired device with nothing being paired). Document the real mechanism
and the two root reasons in the network-stacks guide and the stop_remoted()
docstring.

remote: never leave remoted suspended if tunnel establishment fails

start_tunnel_over_core_device() suspended remoted with a bare
stop_remoted_if_required() and only resumed it after the tunnel came up. If
entering the service-provider context or starting the QUIC/TCP tunnel raised
before that point, resume was skipped -- and a SIGSTOP'd remoted persists past
process exit, breaking Xcode/devicectl until it is manually resumed. Guard the
establishment window with try/finally; resume is idempotent so the early
success-path resume still frees remoted for the tunnel's lifetime.

remote: add macOS-native RSD tunnel and make it the default (no root)

Reach an iOS 17+ device's RSD by piggybacking Apple's own `remoted` tunnel instead
of building one or suspending remoted: ask `com.apple.CoreDevice.remotepairingd`

handshake. All via ctypes + libxpc (no pyobjc). No root, no entitlement, and remoted

sysmon: Add --keep-monitoring to survive relaunches and transient misses

`monitor process` locks onto the identity (uniqueID/startAbsTime/pid) of the
process selected from the first snapshot, and stops the moment that identity is
missing from a sample. That ends collection on an intentional app relaunch, and
on a sampling hiccup where a single snapshot transiently omits the process.

`--keep-monitoring` never locks in an identity: every snapshot re-applies the
`--filter` expressions and resolves the match with `--choose`. A snapshot with
no match is skipped instead of ending the command, and a relaunched process is
picked up on its next sample, with a fresh `Monitoring ...` status line whenever
the resolved instance changes. Default behavior is unchanged.

The flag requires `--choose first|last`: per-snapshot re-selection cannot block
on an interactive prompt, and failing on a transient ambiguity (both the dying
and the new instance visible mid-relaunch) would defeat its purpose.

Closes #1875

device-link: answer DLMessagePurgeDiskSpace instead of aborting the backup

`DLMessagePurgeDiskSpace` is a request, not a fatal error. Apple's own host
(`_DLPurgeDiskSpaceOnComputer` in DeviceLink.framework) builds a dictionary of
`CACHE_DELETE_VOLUME` (the backup root), `CACHE_DELETE_AMOUNT` (`message[1]`,
the bytes the device wants freed) and `CACHE_DELETE_URGENCY_LIMIT`
(`message[2]`), hands it to `CacheDeletePurgeSpaceWithInfo()`, then replies with
a `DLMessageStatusResponse` and keeps serving the connection either way.

We raised `NotEnoughDiskSpaceError` without answering at all, which killed the
link and replaced the device's own diagnosis with a guess. Mirror Apple's
purge-failed path instead (status -1, "DLPurgeDiskSpace failed to purge", zero
bytes reclaimed) and log the requested amount, so the device gets to speak.

Measured on an iPhone18,4 running iOS 26.6.1 by reporting a controlled figure
for `DLMessageGetFreeDiskSpace`:

    reported     asked for       sum
     1048576    2334848147    2335896723
    67108864    2268787859    2335896723
   134217728    2201678995    2335896723

so `CACHE_DELETE_AMOUNT` is `required - reported` against a per-device
constant. After the reply the device reports what it actually wants:

    ['DLMessageProcessMessage', {'ErrorCode': 105,
      'ErrorDescription': 'Insufficient free disk space on drive to back up
       (MBErrorDomain/105)'}]

Also log the figure reported for `DLMessageGetFreeDiskSpace` at debug level --
that is the number the device compares against, and it was missing from every
bug report so far.

device-link: report the free space the device actually requires

DLMessagePurgeDiskSpace's CACHE_DELETE_AMOUNT is not the backup's space
requirement -- it overstates it by a flat 2 GiB. Logging it raw left users to
reverse-engineer the real threshold from two runs (#1879), and the subsequent
MBErrorDomain/105 refusal surfaced as a raw dict repr.

-[MBDriveBackupEngine _prepareFreeSpace] computes required = uploadSize +
128 MiB, proceeds only when the reported figure exceeds it, and otherwise asks
the host to purge (required - reported) + 2 GiB. So the requirement is
recoverable as amount + reported - 2 GiB. Derive it, log it, and attach it to
the 105 refusal; fall back to the raw request when the figures don't fit the
model, so an untested iOS version degrades to today's message instead of
printing a wrong number.

105 now raises NotEnoughDiskSpaceError, which #1884 orphaned when it removed
the unconditional raise from purge_disk_space(). It subclasses
PyMobileDevice3Exception, so existing handlers are unaffected.

The derivation and the strict comparison are documented in purge_disk_space()
against the binary they were read from, with the measurements that confirm
them.

device-link: explain why the requirement can exceed the device's used space

A 256 GB iPhone demanding ~967 GB reads as a bug until you see how the figure is
accumulated. -[MBDriveBackupEngine _addFileToUploadAndMove:flags:] tags each
upload operation with bit 0 when the file hardlinks an already-seen inode and
bit 1 when it clones an already-seen cloneID; addOperation: adds op.size to
_sizeByType regardless, and to _sizeExcludingHardlinksAndClonesForType only when
both bits are clear. _prepareFreeSpace gates on the former.

That is not an over-estimate on the device's part: upload_files writes each file
to its own path under the backup root, so a device-side clone family really does
land as N full copies. Say so in the error rather than leaving users to conclude
the device is lying.

webinspector: let the CDP bridge drive JSContext debuggables

`cdp` listed only WebKit page targets, so an inspectable JSContext - which
`js-shell` and Safari both offer - was invisible. Listing it is not enough:
JavaScriptCore's inspector implements no Target domain, so nothing is announced
on attach, messages are exchanged un-multiplexed (replies carry a top-level id
and arrive on the inspector's result table, not as target events), it announces
no execution context, and it gates console output behind Console.enable - which
Chrome's JavaScript-only frontend never sends.

- List WIRTypeJavaScript targets, as Chrome's "node" target type, pointed at its
  JavaScript-only DevTools frontend (js_app.html), and titled after the process
  hosting them since they share the name "JSContext" and have no URL.
- Qualify target identifiers with the application: page identifiers are numbered
  per application, so every JSContext is page 1 and they used to collide.
- Talk to such a target directly, under wire ids of the bridge's own so the
  shared result table cannot mismatch replies.
- Synthesize the execution context the frontend requires before it evaluates
  anything, and enable WebKit's Console domain on its behalf.

webinspector: queue forwarded events per session

Events carry no id, so a consumer cannot tell its own from another's by
content, yet every receive loop popped from one shared list: whichever woke
first consumed the other's events. Two DevTools sessions on the same bridge -
two JSContexts, or two Safari tabs - lost console output, script and network
events to each other; one of them saw everything twice and the other nothing.

`webinspectord` tags every forwarded message with the session it belongs to
(`WIRDestinationKey`, present for page targets as well as JSContexts), so queue
them per session and hand each consumer its own queue.

webinspector: keep the CDP landing page's target list current

The list was rendered once, so a tab opened or closed on the device - or a
JSContext that only became inspectable afterwards - needed a manual reload to
show up. Poll the target list from the page and re-render it in place, at the
same interval the browser endpoint already uses for target discovery, and only
while the page is the visible tab so a forgotten background tab does not keep
listing the device.

Rendering client-side also drops the titles and URLs the device reports out of
the markup; escape them in the server-rendered list too.

webinspector: drop pages that closed from the cached listing

An application's listing is its complete set of pages, not a delta, but it was
merged into the cached one without ever removing what it no longer mentions.
Every tab ever opened stayed listed for the rest of the session: `webinspector
cdp` accumulated dead targets that could not be attached to, and the browser
endpoint never announced a Target.targetDestroyed.

Replace the application's pages with what the listing reports, updating the ones
that survive in place - sessions hold references to them. Attaching to a page
that closed between being listed and being clicked now closes the websocket
instead of raising.

webinspector: serve the CDP target listing from live state

Every request to /json blocked for a fixed half second waiting for listings it
had just asked the device for - the entire cost of serving one, measured at
503ms against 3ms of actual work. The landing page then scheduled its next poll
2s after that, so a tab opened on the device took up to 2.5s to appear.

The wait buys nothing: webinspectord pushes a fresh listing on its own whenever
a page opens, closes or navigates, so the cached state is already live. Answer
from it and keep the request only as a nudge for anything that does not announce
itself. Serving /json now takes ~2ms, and the page can poll often enough to feel
immediate.

webinspector: let the CDP bridge drive JSContext debuggables

webinspector: take a held CDP page over instead of waiting behind it

WebKit serves a single inspector session per debuggable, so the CDP bridge
serializes sessions per page with PAGE_LOCKS. The page endpoint accepted the
websocket before acquiring that lock and then waited on it with no timeout, so
a second connection to a page that already had a session blocked forever - with
a successfully accepted websocket, which is exactly what a blank, unresponsive
DevTools window is: no console output, and every expression typed into it
silently swallowed.

A DevTools tab left open in a background tab or another window holds its page
for as long as it lives, so this is not a narrow race. JSContexts take the worst
of it: the debuggable outlives every frontend that ever inspected it, and
js_app.html is nothing but the console, so a blocked session shows up as a
completely empty window.

Hand the page over instead, the way Safari's own Web Inspector does. A new
connection signals the holder through PAGE_TAKEOVERS, then still waits on
PAGE_LOCKS so the old session's WIR teardown completes before the new one's
socket setup (webinspectord ignores a setup that races a teardown). Only the
session holding the page on arrival is asked to step aside, so a burst of
connections that arrive together is still served one after another rather than
evicting each other. The superseded frontend gets its websocket closed, so it
shows a disconnect rather than going quietly dead.

The wait is bounded by PAGE_HANDOVER_TIMEOUT rather than PAGE_LOCK_TIMEOUT: the
handover itself is immediate, but a connection queued behind several others is
legitimate and dropping it would trade one silent failure for another.

webinspector: fetch the fallback DevTools frontend without a proxy

urllib applies proxy configuration to loopback addresses too: neither the
no_proxy default nor macOS' ExceptionsList/"exclude simple hostnames" covers
127.0.0.1, and _launch_local_frontend hands back exactly that numeric form. On a
network with a proxy configured, every asset request for the locally launched
Chrome was therefore sent to the proxy, came back empty, and DevTools opened
blank - while the landing page and the bridge WebSocket kept working, since
browsers bypass loopback implicitly.

Do the same here: fetch anything addressed to this machine through an opener
with an empty ProxyHandler, and leave the hosted build on the default opener so
a proxy that is genuinely needed to reach it is still used.

webinspector: retry a DevTools frontend that could not be resolved

_frontend_base cached its failure as an empty string and then short-circuited on
it, so a single unlucky lookup - an unreachable network, a Chrome that lost the
race to publish its debugging port within the launch window - made every later
/devtools request 404 for the rest of the session, leaving a permanently blank
DevTools window with no way back short of restarting the bridge.

Keep only a resolved base, and let a failed attempt fall through so the next
request tries again. A retry would otherwise leak the previous fallback Chrome
and its throwaway profile, so reap those first; lifespan shutdown now shares
that teardown.

webinspector: retry the connection webinspectord gates after a session

webinspectord admits a new session only about ten seconds after the previous one
started - measured from the previous session's start, so closing early does not
help. Until the gate lifts it accepts the connection but never completes the TLS
handshake, and that is a hair longer than DEFAULT_SSL_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT, so the
handshake aborted at ten seconds flat.

Every reattach that came too soon therefore failed: restarting the CDP bridge,
opening an automation session once inspection was done, or simply running the
Web Inspector tests in sequence, which alternated pass/fail with every other
connection. Worse, a disabled device also terminates the connection, so the
abort was reported as "Web inspector is not enabled" - pointing at a Settings
toggle that was never off.

The attempt that timed out has itself waited the gate out, so retry once, and
only for our own handshake timeout - a device that really did terminate the
connection is still reported as before.

webinspector: reset the CDP bridge's per-page state on every run

PAGE_LOCKS and PAGE_TAKEOVERS live for the process, but the asyncio primitives
in them belong to the event loop that created them, and a page handler killed
without unwinding - a forced shutdown, a loop torn down under it - leaves its
lock held.

Either one carried into a second run in the same process wedged every connection
to that page: it waited out the full PAGE_HANDOVER_TIMEOUT for a lock nobody was
left to release, then failed with "is bound to a different event loop". Running
the Web Inspector tests together hit exactly this - the takeover test hung
indefinitely at 100% CPU behind a lock the previous test's forced server
shutdown had abandoned.

Clear both at lifespan startup: no page can be attached yet at that point, so
each run starts from primitives belonging to its own loop.

webinspector: name the connection already debugging a page

WebKit serves a single inspector session per debuggable, and a page held by
another Web Inspector connection - a second pymobiledevice3, Safari's own Web
Inspector, or a client that exited without detaching - simply never reports an
inspection target. Both attach paths waited the full target-creation timeout and
then blamed the device, which sends people restarting webinspectord or the
phone; the page listing had said who held it the whole time.

Keep WIRConnectionIdentifierKey for web pages the way automation targets already
keep it, and when the target never arrives, name the holder instead.

webinspector: keep the CDP session on its page target

iOS 26 announces a Target.targetCreated per subframe, with type "frame",
but _target_created adopted every announced target as the session's
current one. The session walked off its page target onto the last iframe
and stayed there: a frame target is neither committed nor destroyed while
its page is fine, so nothing ever moved it back.

What the frame target then answers depends on site isolation. In-process
frames reply "Page domain already enabled" and "Missing node for given
nodeId"; a site-isolated frame runs FrameInspectorController, which has no
Page/Network/Audit at all - and with site isolation off registers no agents
whatsoever, so every request comes back as

    -32601 'Runtime' domain was not found

for Runtime, Network, Page, CSS, Debugger and Audit alike, and the session
is dead for the rest of its life. Note this is a distinct failure from a
target that went away, which answers -32000 "Missing target for given
targetId" and is already handled.

So route the session only to targets announced as pages, in create() as
well - a frame target is announced as early as attach time, and can be the
first targetInfo a session sees. Track which targets were adopted, so a
subframe going away no longer fires a load event and a document update that
reset panels the frontend filled from the page.

Reproduced and verified on iPhone99,11 / iOS 26.6.1 with Chrome's DevTools
frontend attached to a Safari tab, on a page with cross-origin iframes.

common: Follow the XDG Base Directory Specification on Linux (#1891)

On Linux, fresh installations now place pymobiledevice3's home folder at
$XDG_DATA_HOME/pymobiledevice3, defaulting to ~/.local/share/pymobiledevice3
when the variable is unset or relative, as the spec requires. An existing
~/.pymobiledevice3 is preferred and keeps being used, so current setups are
unaffected; macOS and Windows are unchanged (Wsl inherits the Linux behavior).

Path resolution lives in the OsUtils platform layer: a new
OsUtils.get_home_folder_path() returns the legacy location by default and
Linux overrides it with the XDG logic. get_home_folder() still owns creation
and sudo handling: intermediate directories created by mkdir(parents=True)
under sudo are chowned back to the invoking user, bounded to the invoking
user's home with both sides realpath-normalized so a symlinked home (e.g.
/home -> /var/home) is handled, and the leaf chown stays unconditional so an
interrupted sudo run self-heals. Probes use is_dir() so a stray file at the
home-folder path still fails loudly.

Fixes #1601

tunneld: Add /connect websocket endpoint exposing the tunnel over HTTP (#1893)

Clients that cannot reach the tunnel interface tunneld created — e.g.
tunneld running in a different docker network stack, or on a different
host altogether — cannot use the RSD addresses reported over GET /. The
new WS /connect?udid=<UDID>[&port=<PORT>] endpoint bridges such clients
into the tunnel through the HTTP API instead: binary websocket messages
are forwarded as-is over a TCP connection opened on the device's tunnel
address (port defaults to the tunnel's RSD port), and vice versa, until
either side disconnects.

- Application close codes: 4404 (no tunnel for that UDID), 4502 (TCP
  connection over the tunnel failed), 1003 (text frame on the binary
  bridge), 1013 (over the 200 concurrent-bridge cap)
- uvicorn now runs with ws='wsproto' (already a runtime dependency) and
  per-message deflate disabled, since the bridged tunnel traffic is
  mostly encrypted and incompressible
- TunneldCore.get_tunnel() carries the dashless-UDID normalization
  (#1388), so /connect also accepts UDIDs as reported by Linux usbmuxd

Fixes #1648

tunneld: Remove unix-domain-socket binding (--uds)

The feature was stale by design: --uds only ever moved the HTTP control
channel onto a unix socket, while the data plane - the RSD dials to the
reported tunnel-address:tunnel-port - always relied on TCP, so it never
delivered a pure-unix path.

- remote tunneld loses --uds; TunneldRunner binds TCP only
- TunneldAddress narrows to (host, port); the UDS client transport
  (_UnixHTTPConnection) is gone
- a --tunnel value with a non-numeric :suffix now fails with a clear
  BadParameter naming the removal, instead of being treated as a socket
  path

tunneld: Reach remote tunneld instances through the /connect bridge

pymobiledevice3 now consumes the WS /connect endpoint itself, so every
command and library consumer works against a tunneld whose tunnel
interface is unreachable from the client - tunneld in a different docker
network stack, on another host, or behind an SSH port-forward.

- TunneldConnectDialer: an asyncio.open_connection-compatible dialer
  (the seam RemoteServiceDiscoveryService already exposes for the
  userspace tunnel) that bridges each device-bound connection through
  /connect. The caller gets one end of a socket.socketpair whose other
  end is pumped against the websocket - a real socket, so
  ServiceConnection's get_extra_info('socket') contract holds. Each
  pump ends when either leg closes, so closing the RSD tears down
  every bridge; nothing needs explicit teardown.
- get_tunneld_devices()/get_tunneld_device_by_udid() take
  bridge=None|bool: None bridges automatically when the tunneld host is
  non-loopback; True forces it for addresses that only look local
  (SSH port-forwards).
- --tunnel accepts UDID@HOST[:PORT] (IPv6 in brackets), which forces
  the bridge; a tunneld that predates /connect fails with a clear
  upgrade message.

Verified end-to-end against a real tunneld server (uvicorn/wsproto)
bridging into a local TCP echo server, including through
ServiceConnection.create_using_tcp.

tunneld: Bound upstream federation with a hop budget

Tunnelds that register each other (A -> B -> A) recursed on every GET /:
the nesting spawned a growing tree of in-flight requests against the
bounded to_thread executor, and the innermost fetches lost the race
against their parents' 2s timeout - so a cycle dropped the very listings
it was meant to merge. With two mutually registered tunnelds, each one's
listing was missing the other's device.

Federated requests now carry x-tunneld-hops-remaining (default 4),
decremented per hop and not forwarded at zero, and entries reported
through several paths are listed once.

Verified with two real federated tunneld servers: the peer's device is
now present (it was missing before) and each tunnel appears once.

tunneld: Relay /connect to the upstream that owns the device

Federating another tunneld only merged its listing, and the addresses in
that listing are ULAs on the upstream host's utun - reachable only from a
client that already had L3 connectivity to that host. So federation
presupposed a VPN or hand-rolled routes, which is why a device discovered
through an aggregator was a dead end.

The /connect bridge removes that prerequisite. A /connect for a device
none of this instance's own tunnels serve is now relayed to the upstream
that owns it, so a client needs a route to one tunneld and nothing else:

    sudo pymobiledevice3 remote tunneld --host 0.0.0.0 \
        --upstream http://lab-1:49151 --upstream http://lab-2:49151
    pymobiledevice3 developer dvt ls / --tunnel 'UDID@front:49151'

- new --upstream (repeatable) seeds the set POST /upstream manages
- GET / entries carry an origin: null when served directly, else the URL
  of the hop that reported them, so a client that can reach that upstream
  may skip the relay
- the upstream's own close code is passed through, so 4404/4502 name the
  tunneld that actually refused
- the /connect client is now shared (tunneld/ws_bridge.py) between the
  dialer and this relay rather than hand-rolled twice

Verified against a real device: an aggregator holding no tunnels of its
own fronted a separate tunneld process and served dvt ls / and
device-information over the two-hop path, with no tracebacks on either
instance.

tunneld: Validate and canonicalize upstream URLs

Federation reads an upstream address twice - requests fetches the listing
from the URL, while the /connect relay dials the host and port parsed out
of it - and the two disagreed on everything except the exact spelling
'http://HOST:PORT':

- a schemeless 'lab-1:49151' (the spelling --tunnel UDID@HOST:PORT
  invites) parses as scheme 'lab-1' with no host: the listing fetch threw
  InvalidSchema into a debug log and the relay refused, so registering
  one did nothing at all, silently
- an https:// upstream fetched its listing over TLS but was relayed to in
  plaintext, on port 80 when no port was given
- a URL carrying a path fetched that path but relayed to the bare host

Registration now runs both spellings through one normalizer, which fills
in tunneld's default port, brackets IPv6 literals, and rejects what
neither path could act on (non-http scheme, no host, a path or query, a
bad port). --upstream reports the failure as a usage error and
POST /upstream as a 400, instead of accepting an address that quietly
never works. HOST, HOST:PORT and http://HOST[:PORT] are all accepted and
stored canonically, so GET /upstream and DELETE /upstream agree.

tunneld: Address /connect at a tunnel, not just a device

A device can have more than one tunnel: when a tunneld federates another
that monitors the same host, its listing carries both its own tunnel and
the federated one for that UDID. /connect keyed on the UDID alone, so it
paired whichever tunnel it found locally with the port the caller asked
for - dialing one tunnel's address at another's port, an endpoint that
exists nowhere:

    4502 failed to connect to [fdc9:ec7b:4fdf::1]:63727: [Errno 61]
         Connect call failed

/connect now takes an optional ?address=, the tunnel address the caller
means. A local tunnel is used only when it matches; otherwise the request
falls through to the upstream that serves that exact tunnel, so holding
our own tunnel to a device no longer hides another instance's. The dialer
names the tunnel it is bridging for, and the relay passes it upstream.
Older tunnelds ignore the parameter and keep their UDID-only behaviour.

Docs: a front tunneld on a host that also has devices attached should run
with the monitors off, or it federates a device it is also serving and
lists it twice.

Verified against a real device in that exact topology: an aggregator
holding its own tunnel plus a federated one now serves dvt ls / over
either, where both previously failed.

tunneld: Fix the connect-refused test hanging on macOS CI

The test held a socket bound but not listening and connected to its port,
expecting an RST. macOS does not send one - it drops the SYN silently -
so tunneld burned its whole CONNECT_TCP_TIMEOUT before answering 4502,
and on the slower macOS runners the test client's own recv timeout fired
first: 'socket.timeout: timed out' on py3.9/macos-latest.

Connect to a released port instead, which does get an RST. The file drops
from 9.3s to 1.5s as a side effect. A port stolen in the gap makes the
assertion fail loudly rather than pass silently.

mobile_image_mounter: survive the CopyDevices hangup on legacy devices

The is_image_mounted() CopyDevices fallback (added for the iOS 27.0
empty-ImageSignature quirk) broke mounting on legacy devices: their
mobile_storage_proxy (observed on iOS 12.5.7) answers the unknown
command with UnknownCommand and then hangs up the connection, so the
next command - upload_image()'s ReceiveBytes - failed with
ConnectionResetError('Connection lost').

When CopyDevices turns out unsupported, drop the hung-up connection so
the next command transparently reconnects, and remember the command is
unsupported so later mounted-checks in the same flow do not provoke the
hangup again.

Fixes #1897

web_protocol: Support Playwright connectOverCDP against a WKWebView

Attaching Playwright (chromium.connectOverCDP) to an already-loaded page
over `webinspector cdp` completed the handshake but never evaluated, and
DevTools-only translation left several Chrome-protocol contracts unmet:

- Page.getFrameTree is now answered from the resource tree (WebKit only
  implements Page.getResourceTree), tolerating the no-params form Playwright
  sends.
- Page.setLifecycleEventsEnabled is acknowledged instead of raw-forwarded
  (WebKit has no such method and errored).
- The browser endpoint's target-info now carries a browserContextId, which
  CRBrowser asserts on before adopting a page.
- Runtime.executionContextCreated now carries auxData (isDefault + frameId),
  which a CDP client needs to bind the context to its frame and main world;
  without it the context was never registered and every evaluate hung.
- /json/version/ (trailing slash, which Playwright requests) returns the
  version dict instead of falling through to the target listing.
- The top frame's id is reconciled with the page targetId in both
  directions everywhere a frameId crosses the wire; Chrome guarantees they
  match and a client throws "Frame has been detached" otherwise.
- Isolated worlds (Page.createIsolatedWorld) are synthesized and their
  evaluations rerouted to the page's main world, so page.title()/locator
  reads (which run in Playwright's utility world) no longer hang.

Adds a device test exercising the full flat-session handshake.

tests: answer the CDP server's websocket keepalive pings

The test client read frames off the socket but never answered a Ping, so
uvicorn closed any connection whose session outlived its ping timeout with
"keepalive ping timeout" - failing the test on a websocket close rather
than on anything it set out to check. Pong every ping.

web_protocol: Report the navigation lifecycle to CDP clients

WebKit reports a load's progress with the events Chrome replaced years ago,
so a modern CDP client saw a navigation happen and never learned it had
finished. Two contracts were missing, and together they hung every
navigating call (page.goto, page.reload, waitForNavigation) until its
timeout:

- Page.lifecycleEvent was never emitted. Clients wait on it and ignore the
  Page.loadEventFired/domContentEventFired that WebKit does send, and
  Page.setLifecycleEventsEnabled was acknowledged without doing anything.
  Each real signal is now also reported as the lifecycle event it
  corresponds to, once a client asks for them.
- Page.navigate answered without a loaderId, which is how a client tells a
  new-document navigation from an in-page one; without it Playwright waits
  for a same-document navigation that a real page load never reports. The
  navigation now waits for the document it started to commit and answers
  with its loaderId (and still answers without one when nothing commits,
  which is exactly right for a fragment change). That wait runs off the
  input loop so the rest of the session keeps being served meanwhile.

Reported in #1902.

web_protocol: Implement the CDP screenshot methods

Chrome's screenshot path is Page.getLayoutMetrics - which supplies the clip
rectangle and the device pixel ratio - followed by Page.captureScreenshot.
WebKit implements neither, so page.screenshot() died on the first of them
before a capture was ever attempted.

Both are synthesized: the metrics by measuring the page's viewport and
scroll size, and the capture from WebKit's own Page.snapshotRect (the call
the screencast already uses), whose data URL is unwrapped into the bare
base64 payload the client decodes.

Reported in #1904.

web_protocol: Implement the CDP interaction methods

Before every click, fill or hover, a Chrome client brings the target into
view with DOM.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded and then picks the point to act on out
of the quads DOM.getContentQuads returns. WebKit implements neither, and
Playwright treats the resulting "was not found" as a retryable condition -
so every interaction spun in its actionability loop until the caller's
timeout, with nothing surfaced to explain why.

Both are synthesized in-page: the element is scrolled into view through its
remote object, and its border boxes are measured into the flattened corner
quads the client expects. A detached node and one without a layout box are
reported with the messages the client distinguishes, rather than looking
like an unimplemented method.

Reported in #1903.

web_protocol: Keep each frame in its own execution context

WebKit announces one main-world execution context per frame, and they are
not interchangeable. The bridge kept only the most recently announced one
as "the page's" context, and routed every synthesized isolated world to it
regardless of the frame the world was created for. So the moment a subframe
loaded - an ad, a payment iframe - evaluations meant for the main frame
silently started running inside that subframe, where a client's helper
objects do not exist, and its reads came back undefined.

Contexts are now tracked per frame: an isolated world evaluates in the real
context of the frame it was created for, and only the top frame's context
is the page's default.

Verified against a device: with a same-origin child frame injected, the main
frame's isolated world answered `window === window.top` with false before
this change and true after.

web_protocol: Tag remote objects with the subtype Chrome reports

Chrome sets RemoteObject.subtype for the built-in kinds a client dispatches
on; WebKit reports only a className for most of them, so those objects
arrived looking like ordinary ones. The consequential omission is "promise":
a client uses it to tell a value it still has to resolve from a plain
object, and without it reads a result that is not there yet.

Objects WebKit does classify itself keep its answer, and a page's own class
is left a plain object - Chrome keys off the internal type, not the name.

web_protocol: Type text a CDP client sends into the page

WebKit has no Input domain, and neither shape a client uses to type reached
the page - both failing silently, with every call reporting success, so a
form stayed empty while a test believed it had filled it:

- Input.insertText (what fill() and keyboard.insertText() send) was
  swallowed by the blanket acknowledgement for the absent Input domain.
- A character carried on a keyDown event typed nothing. Only the "char"
  event DevTools sends was handled, and Playwright never sends one at all -
  it puts the character in keyDown's own text field.

The character is now taken from whichever event carries it and typed
exactly once: a keyDown's text is held, a "char" supersedes it, and it is
typed on keyUp when no "char" follows - so a client sending both does not
type twice. Keys that perform an action rather than producing text keep
their existing handling.

Text is written through the prototype's own value setter rather than by
assigning the property, because a framework that tracks its inputs only
notices a change made that way; assigning left the field looking filled
while the application still believed it was empty.

Reported in #1907.

web_protocol: Refuse an isolated world for a frame we cannot reach

An isolated world asked for a frame whose execution context this session
never saw fell back to the top frame's, so a client that explicitly asked
about a cross-origin child frame was quietly answered about the main
document instead - it read a real, plausible result for the wrong page.

Refuse it instead. WebKit debugs a cross-origin child through a target of
its own, which this session does not adopt, so the honest answer is that
the frame is not reachable rather than a confident wrong one.

Reaching those frames at all needs the frame targets adopted, which is its
own piece of work; see #1908.

web_protocol: Make child frames reachable by CDP clients

A client builds its frame model from the live attach/navigate pair and only
walks the frame tree once, when it attaches. WebKit never sends
Page.frameAttached, so every child frame that appeared afterwards - or was
recreated by a reload - stayed invisible: page.frames() never grew, and a
navigation reported for a frame the client did not know was discarded.

Three things were missing, and all three are needed before a client can
reach into a child frame:

- Page.frameAttached is synthesized from the navigation WebKit does report,
  once per frame, and Page.frameDetached forgets it again so a frame that
  comes back is announced afresh. Frames the client already learned from a
  frame tree are not announced twice.
- DOM.describeNode resolves an <iframe> element to the frame it hosts, which
  is how a locator reaches into one. WebKit exposes no handle from an
  element to its frame, so the two are correlated through the frame tree by
  the frame's name, or by the URL it loaded; an ambiguous match is reported
  as no match rather than guessed at.
- A world registered by name through Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument
  is now created in every document that loads, the way Chrome does. A client
  registers the world once and expects to find it in each frame, so a frame
  that appeared later had no world to evaluate in.

Verified against a device: an injected child frame is now reported by
page.frames(), evaluates on its own, and is reachable through
frameLocator(). Reported in #1908.

web_protocol: Reach into child frames the way a CDP client does

Child frames were visible but not usable. Four things stood in the way,
each of which left a client either blind to a frame or acting on the wrong
document:

- The frame tree reported a child's parentId as WebKit's own id for the top
  frame, not the id the client knows it by. A client walks the tree by
  parent, so it dropped the whole subtree - which is why a connection that
  attached after an iframe already existed never saw it, while one that was
  live when the frame appeared did.
- An <iframe> was matched to its frame by name or URL, which a srcdoc or
  about:blank frame has neither of, and which several frames can share.
  The element's position among its document's frames identifies it exactly,
  and the frame tree lists children in that same order.
- Typing was always dispatched at the top document's focused element. With
  the focus inside a child frame that element is the frame itself, so the
  text went nowhere - silently. Typing now follows the focus down, and a
  synthesized mouse event is dispatched in the frame that owns the point,
  with the point translated into that frame's coordinates.
- Boxes and quads were measured in the element's own document while a client
  reads them as page coordinates, and DOM.getBoxModel was translated into a
  highlight rather than answered. Both are now measured properly and shifted
  by where the frame sits, and DOM.getFrameOwner/DOM.resolveNode answer for
  the element that owns a frame.

Verified against a device: a client attaching after a child frame exists now
sees it, reads inside it, and fills a field in it.

Interacting with a node inside a child frame through a locator - click(),
and evaluate() in the frame's main world - still does not work; both need
Chrome's node identity model (backendNodeId, DOM.getDocument, adoption
between worlds), which WebKit does not expose. That is its own work; see
#1908.

web_protocol: Type into the document that truly holds the focus

Finding the focused document by walking down from the top frame relied on
the top document reporting the frame element as focused, which it does not
always do - so typing aimed at a field inside a child frame fell back to
the top document and went nowhere, silently.

Ask instead which document both has focus and has something typeable
focused in it, preferring a child frame over the top, which is only ever
reporting the frame element. The common case - nothing framed, or the focus
already on a field in the attached document - still costs a single
round-trip.

Reported in #1907, for the child-frame case tracked in #1908.

web_protocol: Give every attachment to a page its own CDP session

Attaching to a page that was already attached handed back the existing
session id instead of opening another session. A client numbers its request
ids per session, both starting at one, so two attachments sharing an id
each received the other's answers - which trips an assertion inside the
client and takes the whole connection down, not just the second session.
Playwright reaches this whenever a script opens a raw session alongside the
one it drives the page with (page.context().newCDPSession()), which is the
documented way to work around what this bridge cannot do yet.

Each attachment is now a session of its own onto the one shared target.
Requests are renumbered on the way through so an answer goes back to the
session that asked, under the id it used, and events - which belong to no
request - are reported to every session attached to the page, as a real
backend does. The target is torn down when the last session detaches.

Found while validating against a replica of the page in #1908.

web_protocol: Let a CDP client resolve a node back to a handle

Acting on an element through a locator goes through node identity: a client
describes the element to get a backendNodeId, then resolves that id back to
an object in the context it wants to work in. DOM.describeNode reported no
usable id at all, so the resolve that followed found nothing and every
locator-driven interaction with something inside a child frame retried
until it timed out - click() and evaluate() both, with nothing surfaced to
say why.

WebKit has no node identity that outlives a description, so one is kept
here: a described node is given an id of its own, and resolving that id
answers with the node again. The worlds this bridge hands out are all
backed by the frame's one real execution context, so there is no moving to
do - but the answer must still be a handle of its own, because a client
releases the handle it described from and would otherwise be handed back a
reference it has already dropped.

Verified against a device, on a same-origin child frame and on a
cross-origin one nested inside another frame: click() reaches the button
and evaluate() returns the element's own data, where both previously hung.

Fixes #1910.

web_protocol: Carry a user gesture through to the page

A client marks the calls it makes on the user's behalf as a user gesture.
Chrome names that flag `userGesture` and WebKit `emulateUserGesture`, and
an unrecognized parameter is simply ignored - so every such call reached
the page with no gesture behind it, and anything the platform gates behind
one silently did nothing.

Most visibly: an element inside a cross-origin frame cannot be focused
without a gesture. A client's fill() focuses the field and then types into
whatever holds the focus, so it typed nowhere and left the field empty
while reporting success. This was previously written up as a platform
limitation; it was this missing translation.

Verified against a device with a cross-origin frame: fill() into it now
puts the value in the field, through both frame.locator() and
frameLocator().

docs: Document driving a device from Playwright and Puppeteer

The WebView debugging guide covered Chrome DevTools and VS Code but not
test automation, which is now the larger reason to reach for the bridge: a
web test suite can drive a WKWebView in a real app instead of a simulator
or a desktop browser standing in for one.

Adds a section with a runnable connectOverCDP example, what is supported
(navigation and its waits, typing, clicking, screenshots, network
observation, and child frames including cross-origin ones), and the three
things worth knowing when scripting against a device over USB - the first
interaction with a new frame being slow, per-call latency, and a page whose
framework replaces and minifies the global Promise.

Also corrects the single-session caveat: WebKit allows one inspector
session per page, but a single client may open several CDP sessions onto
it, which is what a script doing newCDPSession() alongside its page does.

cdp: Act on editing keys at keydown - held Backspace, Cmd-A, arrows, Delete

Backspace was acted on at keyUp, so holding it deleted one character no matter how long
it was held: the auto-repeats of a held key arrive as keyDown events and were ignored.
Every key but Enter now goes through one path that acts on each keyDown - repeats
included - and performs the key's editing action in-page, since WebKit has no Input
domain: Cmd/Ctrl-A selects all, the arrows and Home/End move the caret (Shift extends
the selection, Alt moves by word, Cmd by line), Backspace and Delete edit, and typing or
Backspace replace whatever is selected. The keydown is dispatched to the page first, and
keyup on release, so the page's own listeners see every key with its modifiers and a
listener that prevents the default keeps its shortcut, as in a browser.

WebKit on iOS sometimes holds the reply to an evaluation that edits the focused field
until the next message reaches the page; the wait then ran out, the target was declared
unresponsive and every following key was skipped. The key handlers now nudge the page
with a trivial evaluation when a reply is late, which frees it within milliseconds.

cdp: Keep the debugger responsive - free withheld replies, stop the idle spin, fetch big scopes

Debugging a large script over CDP from WebStorm or Chrome hung and crawled. Three
causes, each measured on a device against a ~1 MB script:

1. iOS 26 WebKit occasionally holds the reply to a client request - and the events
   that follow it, such as the Debugger.paused after a step - until the next message
   reaches the page. A console evaluate then hung until the user's next action, and
   half of all step-overs in the large script stalled the same way. The bridge only
   nudged the page for its own in-page key handlers. A single watchdog now runs while
   any forwarded client reply is outstanding: every REPLY_WAKE_TICK it sends one
   throwaway evaluation once a reply is REPLY_WAKE_INTERVAL late (one message flushes
   everything held, so traffic is bounded), and drops a request after
   REPLY_WAKE_MAX_AGE. A prompt reply clears its id before the first interval, so a
   normal request is never nudged. Both page targets and JSContexts (the flat path).

2. The receive loop and the internal-reply waits polled with asyncio.sleep(0), spinning
   a core flat out whenever nothing was pending - 23% of a CPU measured while the
   debugger sat idle at a breakpoint - and drained the per-session queue with
   list.pop(0), O(n) per message. Poll at 1 ms instead (a queued message is still
   handled without sleeping, so throughput is unchanged) and back the queue with a
   deque. Idle now measures ~4%.

3. Runtime.getProperties routed a client's request through the bridge's own
   five-second wait, which also pauses event delivery. The property list of a large
   scope - fetched by the Sources panel on every pause - took WebKit longer than that,
   so it was silently answered with an empty list and nothing reached the client for
   five seconds per step. It is now forwarded without blocking under the client's id
   and translated when the reply arrives: a 45k-variable scope returns in full (~0.9 s).

Also: the manual pause button cannot interrupt a busy loop because WebKit handles
inspector messages on the page's JavaScript thread; it lands when the script next
yields. Documented as a platform limit.

Verified on iOS 26.6.1 with a 1.15 MB script (45k lines): define 0.4 s, breakpoint hit
0.3 s, evaluate-in-scope, all scope properties, step-over/into/out, a breakpoint set by
URL, correct values and completion, an armed manual pause - every step well under a
second, where before a step-over hung ~50% of the time and the scope came back empty.
Covered by two device tests; the non-device suite passes.

cdp: Nudge withheld replies without running JavaScript, and cover the debugger's corners

The watchdog that frees a reply WebKit is withholding (and the in-page key handlers'
own nudge) sent a throwaway Runtime.evaluate. An evaluation is itself a statement, so
it can only ever be a safe nudge by accident: with the Pause button armed, pause-on-
next-statement takes whatever runs next. It did not take that "0" in practice - a bare
literal has no statement pause point - but nothing guarantees that, and the nudge ran
script in the page on every late reply. Re-send Debugger.setBreakpointsActive at its
tracked value instead: a real command with nothing to execute and nothing to change.
Measured: it frees a withheld step (reply and paused event together) in ~10 ms, exactly
as the evaluation did, and it works in a session that never enabled the Debugger.

Three device tests widen the debugging surface under test, each step bounded:

- keeps_an_armed_pause_for_user_code: Pause armed, a reply WebKit needs a second for,
  and the user's code scheduled as a timer's direct callback - the pause must land on
  that code and hold it. (Anything else that runs after arming - an evaluate, even an
  arrow wrapper around the call - takes the pause itself; the test is built around
  that, and navigates to a fresh document first so no timer left by an earlier test on
  the shared page can.)
- steps_through_a_large_file_end_to_end: step over every statement of main() in a
  ~12k-line file with async boundaries, fetching the scopes and a watch at each pause
  as an IDE does. 164 step-overs on a 14k-line file measured with no slow step.
- survives_debugger_edge_cases: rapid step-overs fired without waiting coalesce rather
  than wedge; step-into descends a recursion and step-out climbs back; a breakpoint set
  deep in the file is hit with the argument in scope; pause-on-exceptions lands in the
  throwing function; navigating away while paused leaves the session alive.

cdp: Record a full protocol trace with `webinspector cdp --trace`

Too many CDP bugs surfaced only as one-off editor reports that could not be
reproduced here, because there was no record of what the editor and the device
actually exchanged. `--trace <file>` writes every message, in both directions, on
both sides of the bridge - editor->bridge, bridge->editor, bridge->device,
device->bridge - as one timestamped JSON line each. A page target's messages ride
inside WebKit's Target.* envelopes; the device side records the real inner message
and notes the envelope and target id, so a trace reads as the protocol exchange it
is.

This turns "step-over did not land in WebStorm" into a report anyone can diagnose:
the trace shows exactly which request got no reply, or which reply the editor never
acted on. The recorder never raises into the bridge - a trace that cannot be written
is logged once and abandoned - and flushes per message so a crash loses nothing. A
trace carries page content, evaluation results and script sources; it is documented
as sensitive.

Verified live against a real DevTools frontend on both a JSContext (flat path) and a
Safari page (Target-multiplexed): full editor-request -> device -> reply -> editor
chains recorded, envelopes unwrapped. Unit tests cover the writer, the Target
unwrapping, the inspector device hooks and the page websocket pump.

cdp: Correlate an iframe to its frame by identity, not document order

Resolving an <iframe> element to the frame it hosts (DOM.describeNode, how
frameLocator()/contentFrame() reach into a child frame) paired the nth <iframe>
in the document with the nth child in the frame tree. On iOS 26 the frame tree
orders a document's entries by when each frame was created, not by where its
element sits, so every frame whose DOM position differed from its creation order
resolved to the wrong one - and a client's fill()/click() into a cross-origin
frame drove a different frame than the one addressed while reporting success.

Prefer the name a frame was given, or the URL it loaded, which identify it
outright regardless of order; the code already matched on these but only as a
fallback that positional matching pre-empted. Positional matching stays the last
resort, for a frame a unique name or URL cannot pick out (srcdoc, about:blank, or
several sharing a URL).

Verified on iOS 26.6.1: four child frames created a,b,c,d but placed in the
document d,c,a,b each resolve to their own frame (confirmed by reading
document.URL inside the resolved frame's world), where before every one was off.

cdp: Add the Fetch domain over WebKit interception, for request mocking and Basic auth

WebKit has a request-interception API (Network.addInterception/interceptContinue/
interceptWithRequest and the Network.requestIntercepted event) but Chrome's Fetch
domain, which every automation framework drives, was unimplemented - calling it
returned "'Fetch' domain was not found".

Translate Fetch onto it: Fetch.enable arms WebKit interception for the given URL
patterns; each paused request surfaces as Fetch.requestPaused (enriched with the
frameId and resourceType WebKit omits, cached from Network.requestWillBeSent); and
Fetch.continueRequest/fulfillRequest/failRequest answer it through the matching
Network.intercept* command. This is what Playwright's route() and Puppeteer's
request interception need.

The motivating use is answering HTTP Basic auth with no on-device dialog: injecting
an Authorization header on Fetch.continueRequest for the protected request answers
the challenge before it is raised. WebKit surfaces no auth-challenge event of its
own (the OS dialog owns it), so the reactive Fetch.authRequired/httpCredentials path
cannot fire; the proactive header injection is the supported route, and is
documented as such.

Verified on iOS 26.6.1: Fetch.enable then a fetch() of an httpbin Basic-auth URL
surfaces as Fetch.requestPaused, and continueRequest with an injected Authorization
header returns {"authenticated": true} - no dialog. Covered by a device test.

(cherry picked from commit 7daee22af28ff463c9f1e226d327653662621c3b)

cdp: Emulate user preferences through Page.overrideUserPreference

Chrome's dark-mode emulation was sent to the device as Page.setForcedAppearance, a command WebKit
has since replaced: neither WebKit main nor Safari 26's protocol define it, and iOS 26 answers
"'Page.setForcedAppearance' was not found" while the editor shows the emulation as active. The media
features of Emulation.setEmulatedMedia (prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion,
prefers-contrast) were dropped on the floor as well.

Both now map onto Page.overrideUserPreference, one override per preference, a valueless override
clearing it; features left out of a later setEmulatedMedia are reset as in Chrome, and the latest
override per preference is replayed after a process swap. The stale handler for
Page.defaultAppearanceDidChange (an event that no longer exists) goes away.

Verified on iOS 26: all three preferences flip and clear; an emulated print media type renders
the light scheme whatever the override says, so the device test checks print on its own.

cdp: Drop WebKit's native entry frame from a paused call stack

WebKit puts a native entry frame at the bottom of every paused call stack - scriptId "0",
lineNumber -1 - for the global/native code beneath the script. Chrome's protocol has no such
frame: a Location must name a real script at a non-negative line. js-debug and WebStorm build the
paused stack strictly, and the invalid frame desynced their step handling - after one step-over the
session stopped advancing, while the console still evaluated (the debuggable was fine; the frontend
had given up on the stack).

_debugger_paused now drops any frame whose location is not a real script location and reshapes the
rest as before, keeping the top frame unconditionally so a pause is never frameless. Verified
against `node --inspect`, whose stacks carry only real script frames with valid locations, and on
an iOS 26 JSContext (the native frame is gone from the forwarded pause, stepping unaffected).

cdp: Strip WebKit's InjectedScript harness from a paused call stack

A `debugger;` in WebStorm's console paused, one step-over worked, then stepping stopped advancing
while the console still evaluated. Comparing a WebStorm session against real `node --inspect` (a
logging proxy) with the same console input: node's pause carries a single user frame; the bridge's
carried three - the user's eval frame plus WebKit's InjectedScript harness (`_wrapCall` and an anon
frame in a source-less script). WebKit runs a console evaluation through its InjectedScript, which
is JavaScript and so lands on the call stack; V8 evaluates natively and shows only the user frame.
WebStorm builds the paused stack strictly and, given the phantom frames, gave up stepping after the
first step.

_debugger_paused now drops inspector frames: a frame in a script the bridge hides as internal (its
source carried the InjectedScript marker), or - on a JSContext, whose every real script the bridge
has seen and given a synthetic URL - a frame in a script it never saw parsed. Verified on an iOS 26
JSContext: the console-eval pause now reports the single user frame node does, before and after a
step. (The earlier native-frame drop in this branch is the same stack-cleaning; both land together.)

cdp: Synthesize Debugger.resumed so stepping keeps its paused/resumed alternation

The real reason a WebStorm step-over stopped advancing after the first step: WebKit emits no
Debugger.resumed when a step resumes then repauses - it sends none at all (verified against the
device: zero resumed for two pauses, where node sends one between them). Chrome's protocol
alternates paused/resumed, and WebStorm's step machine waits for the resumed before it will issue
another step; seeing paused-after-paused, it stalled.

The bridge now tracks whether the client believes it is paused and injects a Debugger.resumed
before a pause it is not expecting, so a step reads as paused -> resumed -> paused as it does on
node. A real resumed from the device is forwarded once and clears the state; a stray one while the
client is already running is dropped; a navigation resets it. Verified on an iOS 26 JSContext: the
client now sees paused@1 -> resumed -> paused@2 -> resumed -> ... across a run of step-overs.

its target picker) and then Target.setDiscoverTargets, and waits for the initial Target.targetCreated

regardless of what an earlier getTargets already learnt. Verified end to end with js-debug's

The CDP bugs in this series were all behavioral and editor-specific, found by capturing a real
editor session and diffing it against real node, then fixed - but nothing replayed those sessions
to keep them fixed. A future change could quietly break stepping or attach again, and no test would
notice until a user's editor did.

golden_flow.replay_flat_session drives a real CdpTarget with a recorded session's editor commands
and device responses (a trimmed `webinspector cdp --trace`), and returns what the bridge emits to
the editor. The device inputs are authentic; a test asserts the current, correct output, so a
regression fails offline in CI without a device.

The first fixture is the WebStorm JSContext step-over that stalled: the golden test asserts the
paused stack is the single user frame node reports (WebKit's native and InjectedScript frames
stripped) and that a step reads paused -> resumed -> paused (WebKit emits no resumed of its own).
Removing either fix makes the test fail. A README documents the fixture format and how to capture
more; the harness models the un-multiplexed JSContext path for now.

cdp: Fail cleanly on a device disconnect so --reconnect can retry

When the device restarted or the cable was pulled, the Web Inspector socket died and the bridge
raised ConnectionResetError up the ASGI stack on every landing-page poll - a traceback per request,
forever, with no recovery.

The inspector now notes the loss once and degrades instead of raising on every use: a send with no
live service is a quiet no-op (and never lazily reconnects), the receive task ends cleanly, and
get_open_pages tolerates the failure. It then fires an `on_connection_lost` callback, which the CDP
bridge turns into a clean shutdown and a ConnectionTerminatedError("the device disconnected").

That error is what pymobiledevice3's existing top-level `--reconnect` already handles: it waits for
the device to come back and re-runs the command. So the bridge behaves like every other command -
a disconnect stops it with a clear error by default, and `pymobiledevice3 --reconnect webinspector
cdp ...` reconnects - instead of carrying its own reconnect logic.

cdp: End a child frame's contexts when it commits a new document (#1919)

WebKit reports a child frame's navigation (Page.frameNavigated, from
didCommitLoad) and then announces the new document's main-world context,
but says nothing about the contexts the previous document had. Chrome
announces their end (Runtime.executionContextDestroyed), and a client
relies on that to drop what it built in them.

The bridge forwarded the navigation and the new context only, so a client
kept the synthesized isolated world of the old document, and Playwright
kept using the injected utility script it had created there. Every
locator retry then queried the old, detached document: a field in a
payment iframe that its SDK navigated after the client first touched it
was never found, and fill() timed out with no Input.* call ever made,
while a fresh session that attached after the final document existed
succeeded (#1919).

On a child frame's frameNavigated, announce the end of its main-world
context and its synthesized worlds, forget them so a client that keeps
using one is refused by the device instead of silently answered from the
top frame, and let the worlds the client registered be created afresh for
the new document. A same-document navigation reports no frameNavigated,
so this cannot misfire on an SPA's route changes (verified: six pushState
changes produced none).

Reproduced and verified on an iPhone (iOS 26.6.1) with Playwright 1.62:
an iframe touched while showing its first document, then navigated to a
form, timed out on fill() for 12s before and fills in under 2s after; a
local Chrome fills the same scenario, and the untouched control filled
before the change too. Added an offline test for the event sequence and
a device test for the world re-creation.

cdp: Drive Chrome's Memory and Performance panels from WebKit's profiling domains

The bridge stubbed HeapProfiler.enable and Profiler.enable and forwarded every other
HeapProfiler, Profiler and Tracing method raw, which WebKit rejects with "domain was not
found": the Memory panel's snapshot and collect-garbage buttons, the CPU profiler and the
Performance panel were all dead, although the JSContext docs advertised Memory.

WebKit records the same three things in its own shapes, so translate them
(cdp_profiling.py, pure converters):

- HeapProfiler.takeHeapSnapshot / startTrackingHeapObjects: Heap.snapshot and
  Heap.startTracking's closing snapshot reshaped into V8's heap snapshot document. WebKit
  class names become constructors, its Property/Index/Variable edges V8's
  property/element/context edges, engine internals "hidden"/"code" so the panel groups
  them as (system)/(compiled code). Node ids stay WebKit's so getObjectByHeapObjectId maps
  onto Heap.getRemoteObject. WebKit repeats the root's edge to an object once per reason
  it is retained; the frontend seeds its distance search with one slot per root edge and
  throws "BFS failed" on a repeat, so edges are de-duplicated.
- collectGarbage: Heap.gc. Allocation sampling and getHeapObjectId, which WebKit cannot
  do, are refused with a message the panel shows instead of a domain error.
- Profiler.start/stop: ScriptProfiler.startTracking/stopTracking, with the profile built
  from the trackingComplete samples that follow the stop: a call tree with 0-based
  locations, the inspector's own console-evaluation frames stripped, and idle samples
  inserted across sampling gaps - WebKit samples only while script runs, and Chrome would
  otherwise charge the idle time to the last sampled frame.
- Tracing.start/end on a page: a Timeline recording plus a ScriptProfiler one, delivered as
  Chrome trace events on Tracing.end: browser/renderer metadata and TracingStartedInBrowser
  for the main thread, each timed record under a WebKit RenderingFrame as a main-thread
  task (the frame itself spans idle time), function calls, timers, animation frames, style,
  layout, paint and composite under Chrome's names, console.time spans, screenshots when
  asked, and the CPU profile as Profile/ProfileChunk for the flame chart. A JSContext has
  no Timeline; Chrome's JavaScript-only frontend profiles it through Profiler.start.

Verified on an iOS 26.4 device with the pinned DevTools frontend: heap snapshot with
retainers, allocation timeline, CPU flame chart of a JSContext, and a page recording
with tasks, timings and screenshots. Fixtures are real payloads captured from the device.
