webinspector: Retry a refused handshake instead of reporting it as disabled

webinspectord refuses a session by terminating the connection, and does so
for three reasons that are indistinguishable at the moment they happen: Web
Inspector is disabled, the ten-second gate on consecutive sessions has not
elapsed, or it is not up yet because the device is still booting. Only the
first is permanent, but every one of them was reported as Web Inspector being
disabled - which is fatal to the caller.

That is what `--reconnect` runs into: it re-invokes the command the moment
lockdownd answers again, which is a second or two before webinspectord serves
anything, so a CDP bridge that survived a device reboot then died claiming
Web Inspector was off. Reproduced by rebooting the device under a running
`pymobiledevice3 --reconnect webinspector cdp` (1 in 3 reboots), and directly
by attaching the instant lockdownd answers after a reboot.

Retry the handshake while the device is still there, and report the refusal
as a disabled Web Inspector only once it outlives the deadline; the device's
own disabled notification still ends the wait immediately. A device that went
away mid-handshake is told apart by whether lockdownd still answers, and is
reported as the disconnect it is, so `--reconnect` retries it. This replaces
the single retry that waited out the session gate, which the loop subsumes.

cdp: Connect to the device before uvicorn owns the failure

The bridge connected to WebInspector from inside the ASGI lifespan, and
uvicorn runs the lifespan itself: an exception there is logged as a traceback
and turned into `sys.exit(3)`, which asyncio re-raises straight out of the
event loop. A device error while the bridge was starting therefore killed the
process with exit code 3 before pymobiledevice3's top-level handler ever
classified it, so `--reconnect` never waited for the device and never re-ran
the command - the bridge just died with a traceback.

Reproduced by rebooting the device under a running
`pymobiledevice3 --reconnect webinspector cdp`: three of eight reboots ended
in "Application startup failed. Exiting." and exit code 3. Connecting before
handing the app to uvicorn keeps the error an ordinary exception (the
lifespan's own connect is then a no-op); six of six reboots now reconnect.

remoted's RSD connection to the tunnel address".

directly from an unentitled process yields the same own-uid view whatever

core_device: Drop VRAE:0 from the screen-mirror offer to stop encoder frame drops

The captured Xcode offer declares `FLS;VRAE:0;SW:1;` in the PT=100 codec
bank and pymobiledevice3 replayed it verbatim. `VRAE` is AVConference's
video-resolution-adaptation switch; with it forced off, the device encoder's
only rate-control lever at the fixed 6 Mbps cap is dropping input frames, and
every dropped frame turns the next P-frame into a large residual that the
capped rate controller encodes as the blocky "smear" seen in serve-web and
serve-vnc during motion.

Measured on iPhone18,4 / iOS 27.0 with the device's own VCPEnc telemetry over
identical 20 s home-screen swipe sequences: `VRAE:0` present drops 207-219
frames per run (Tx ~42 fps); `FLS;SW:1;` drops none (Tx ~53 fps). In Chrome
via serve-web the old string produced repeated multi-frame mosaic episodes;
the new default produced none across two runs. LTRP, FEC and `SW:1` do not
change the drop count. The device intersects the offered token list with the
ones it knows (`VRAE`, `SW`) and silently discards the rest, which is why
jkcoxson/idevice's richer string also works: it simply omits `VRAE:0`.

Also expose `hevc_features` / `avc_features` overrides on
`DisplayService.start_video_stream()` so the strings can be experimented with
from scripts, keep the captured string for the byte-equivalence self-check,
and record the finding in MOTION_TEAR_FINDINGS.md.

core_device: Stop media streams on a fresh RemoteXPC connection

serve-web / serve-vnc left the device wedged after Ctrl-C: Camera and
Voice Memos stayed blocked and screen mirroring would not re-arm until a
reboot. Xcode's Device Hub tore down cleanly.

Root cause: our stop reused the RemoteXPC connection that had already
issued the stream `start`. A RemoteXPC connection tolerates only one
reply-bearing request; the second makes dtremotedisplayd fatally assert
("Attempted to send non-reply msg N on the reply channel") and SIGABRT
*before* it runs its teardown -- stopRemoteObservation, releasing the
audit activity assertion, and stopping the screen-sharing indicator --
so the device stayed "observed remotely" with its sensors held. The
`stop_media_stream` "IncompleteReadError == success" comment was masking
that crash, and its `{avcMediaStreamOptionClientSessionID: <uuid>}`
payload never decoded to the daemon's StopRequest in the first place.

Fix:
- Send the correct CoreDevice StopRequest payload (stopAll: Bool,
  identifiers: [UInt32]?), mined from the DDI.
- Add DisplayService.stop_all_streams(), which issues the stop as the
  sole request on a brand-new connection.

web_protocol: Await any thenable a client asks to await, as Chrome does

A client that calls Runtime.callFunctionOn with awaitPromise expects the
result resolved the way Promise.resolve does: any thenable is followed.
WebKit awaits only a native promise and hands anything else back as-is,
so a page that replaced the global Promise with a class of its own - as
zone.js does on every Angular app - answered the call with the promise
object where the value should be. Playwright's page.screenshot() read that
and failed with '"undefined" is not valid JSON' (#1904).

Adopt a thenable result through an async function, which yields a native
promise whatever the page did to its Promise binding, and let WebKit await
that. Non-thenable results are untouched and no round-trip is added.

The subtype tagging added earlier for #1904 was not what this path needed:
the client never inspects the subtype, and Chrome tags only native
promises anyway. The guide said `await` still behaved on such pages; it
did not, and now does.

pasteboard: Stop clipboard sync stalling for a minute on rich copies

dtpasteboardd resolves the representations of a copy one by one, and an app
may advertise a type it cannot produce. Notes does: its public.rtf fails only
after a ~64 s timeout. An AUTONOTIFY subscriber makes the daemon do that full
resolve on every change before it sends the PUSH, whatever dataPolicy the
subscription names, and every other request queues behind it. So with sync on,
text copied in Notes reached the host a minute late and GET /clipboard hung
meanwhile.

PasteboardMonitor no longer subscribes. It observes the
com.apple.pasteboard.notify.changed Darwin notification and reads the
pasteboard with a promiseSecondary PULL, which the daemon answers at once with
the primary type of each item. Everything is pulled only when that yields
nothing to share and a picture is promised in a secondary type. Its own SETs
are recognised by the change count of their SET_REPLY. GET /clipboard of
serve-web reads the same way.

pasteboard: Don't fail a copy to the device while the daemon is busy

PasteboardMonitor waited up to 5 s for the SET_REPLY. While dtpasteboardd
resolves a rich copy it answers nothing for a minute, so a host copy made in
that window failed (HTTP 500 from serve-web) although the daemon applied it as
soon as it was free.

The SET is now sent and its reply read in the background; the reply only
serves to recognise the change the SET causes. The monitor lets a pending reply
be read before it decides whose copy a change is.

pasteboard: Never make the device pasteboard daemon stall

Reading a picture that a rich-text app keeps inside its web archive (a picture
copied in Notes) needed a PULL of every representation, which blocks
dtpasteboardd for about a minute: nothing else, in either direction, got
through meanwhile. The daemon has no request for a single type (a host RESOLVE
loads every representation before the one it names), so that read is now off
unless allow_full_pull asks for it, and such a copy is not shared.

Apple's own `devicectl device pasteboard monitor` reports a Notes text copy
after 64 s for the same reason; the module docstring records what the daemon
does per policy.

policy_threshold() used the wrong wire key (`_0`); the daemon decodes the
limit as `bytes`.

new one arrives. Since iOS 27.2 it also compares the newcomer's handshake

    ConnectionRefusedError(61, "Connect call failed ...")

on a tunnel -- even after that peer disconnected -- and re-attaches when the
next peer presents a different one ("Peer UUID changed across reconnect;
reattaching so clients re-discover it"), closing every service listener it
advertised, to the newcomer and to earlier peers alike. Every RSD connection
sent a fresh random UUID, so anything joining an existing tunnel failed right
after the handshake:

    $ pymobiledevice3 remote rsd-info --rsd fd88:51e2:a06c::1 60658

reconnecting with its own UUID, so no other identity survives there), and
the deterministic pairing host id elsewhere. The remotectl helpers move from
native_tunnel to remotexpc, which native_tunnel already depends on.

remotepairing: Match bonjour answers to pair records by authTag

get_remote_pairing_tunnel_services() found the device behind a
_remotepairing._tcp answer by trying every RemotePairing record against
every address of every answer: a TCP connect, a handshake and a failed
pair-verify per guess, aimed at every Apple device on the network. tunneld
repeats that every 5 seconds, including for devices it already tunnels.

The advert is built to avoid this: its TXT record carries an opaque
identifier and an authTag = SipHash-2-4(altIRK, identifier), and the device
hands its altIRK to the host in the M6 identity payload of pair-setup. We
discarded it. Record it in the pair record (peer_alt_irk, the key the
device-initiated records already use) and match answers offline, so only
paired devices are contacted, each with its own record. tunneld passes the
devices it already serves as excluded_identifiers so they are skipped
before connecting.

Records written before this change hold no altIRK and cannot be matched; a
one-time warning names the file to delete before pairing again (promptless
over USB with `lockdown remotepairing --pair`).

lockdown: Look a mobdev2 device up by its record's WiFiMACAddress only

get_mobdev2_lockdowns(udid=...) narrowed the pair records to the requested
device but still opened a lockdown connection to every advertised device
that had no record, returning all of them (`--mobdev2 --udid X` could even
prompt between unrelated devices). It also only knew records cached in our
own folder, so a device paired through usbmuxd was never recognized.

A mobdev2 instance name starts with the device's Wi-Fi MAC and the pair
record holds WiFiMACAddress, so when a udid is given connect only to the
matching answer, resolve the record through get_preferred_pair_record()
when it is not cached locally, and skip the browse when there is no record
to recognize the device by.

remotexpc: Resolve the handshake UUID before remoted is suspended

Since 616eada3 every RSD handshake on macOS identifies itself with the host
remoted's UUID, read from `remotectl dumpstate` -- once per connection.
remotectl gets its answer from remoted, and the RSD-over-bonjour path
(get_rsds, used by `remote start-tunnel` and tunneld) connects while remoted
is SIGSTOPped. Each handshake therefore sat out remotectl's 10 second
timeout, the endpoint was skipped at debug level, and

    $ sudo pymobiledevice3 remote start-tunnel --no-native
    INFO No tunnel services discovered, trying again

Resolve the identity once per process (it is only useful while it stays the
same anyway) and have stop_remoted_if_required() resolve it before it
suspends remoted.

lockdown: Match mobdev2 adverts to paired hosts by authTag

A mobdev2 advert names its device by a MAC that is randomized whenever the
device uses a private Wi-Fi address, so since v11.16.1 a device no record
names is offered every pair record -- including devices that were never
paired with us.

The advert does say which hosts the device is paired with: its TXT record
carries an opaque identifier and one tag per paired host (authTag,
authTag#1, ...), each HMAC-SHA256(HKDF-SHA512(HostID), identifier)[:8].
That is what MobileDevice's AMDIsTXTRecordForUDID checks, and it needs
nothing beyond the HostID already in every lockdown pair record.

Offer a device only the records of the hosts it names, and skip a device
that names none of ours without contacting it. A host pairs every device
under one HostID, so the tag cannot tell our own devices apart; among those
the device still picks its record by accepting it. Adverts without tags
(older iOS) are handled as before.

safe_paths: Keep device-supplied names and paths beneath a host directory

A paired device hands the host strings that end up as host paths: backup file
names, logarchive members, provisioning profile UUIDs, the device identifier
itself. Nothing checked them. resolve_device_path() joins such a string onto
a root and refuses anything that would leave it (absolute paths of either
flavour, ".." components, NULs, and - via a resolve() check - links inside
the root that point out of it); validate_device_filename() requires a single
component; device_file_path() is the common "root / (name + suffix)" case.
DevicePathError is what all of them raise, and the CLI reports it as a
message rather than a traceback.

Colons are deliberately allowed in a filename: a TCP lockdown client is keyed
by its hostname, which is an IPv6 address for a device found over Wi-Fi.

Reworked from the helper besendorf contributed in GHSA-g7ph-v4p5-xwv3. The
original rejected colons and Windows reserved names via
PurePath.is_reserved(), which is deprecated on 3.13 and gone on 3.15.

mobilebackup2: Constrain device paths to the backup root

DeviceLink dispatched every path the device sent - download, upload, move,
copy, remove, list, mkdir - straight onto root_path, so a device could name
"../../.bashrc" and have the host read, overwrite or delete it. Every handler
now goes through resolve_device_path(), and the UDID the device reports,
which becomes the per-device backup directory, must be a single component.

Maintainer rework: the original also walked each path for symlinks and
pre-scanned trees before move/copy. A device cannot create links on the host
and resolve_device_path() already refuses a link that leaves the root, so
that layer is dropped.

than a file in the directory: a backup payload named that way is silently
discarded, CON blocks on the console, COMn touches a serial port. The advisory
fork rejected these via PurePath.is_reserved(), which is gone on Python 3.15;
spell the DOS device names out instead, on every platform, since no device
ever legitimately names a file after one.

Found by running the public test matrix over the advisory merge, which the
workflow (pull_request only) had not done.

userspace_tunnel: Fall back to mobdev2 Wi-Fi when no USB device is attached

When create_using_usbmux() fails because no USB device is connected,
the no-root tunnel provider now falls back to the mobdev2 Wi-Fi path
via get_mobdev2_lockdowns() -- but only when:

- An explicit serial (--udid) was provided, and
- That serial has a known lockdown pair record.

Without a serial, the original usbmux error is re-raised immediately
(no bonjour browse delay). If the fallback finds no mobdev2 service,
the original usbmux exception is re-raised so the CLI surfaces a
clear 'device not found' instead of wandering off to tunneld.

Only NoDeviceConnectedError, DeviceNotFoundError, and
ConnectionFailedToUsbmuxdError trigger the fallback; pairing errors
(PasswordRequiredError, PairingDialogResponsePendingError, etc.)
propagate unchanged.

This enables Wi-Fi-only workflows on hosts whose usbmuxd lacks
network-device support (e.g. stock libimobiledevice usbmuxd on Linux,
or the Microsoft Store 'Apple Devices' app's AMDS on Windows).

Also refactors bonjour.py: shared _browse_receive_loop() /
_assemble_instances() separate full-window collection (browse_service,
byte-identical to pre-iter results) from early-exit snapshots
(iter_browse_service). iter_browse_mobdev2 is now a plain function.

Tests cover the fallback scenarios, multi-packet mDNS aggregation,
and early-exit timing with scripted packets.

bonjour: Fix the lint findings instead of suppressing them

browse_service() assembled nothing in its drain loop and carried a
`# noqa: B007` for the unused loop variable; assembling inside the body
drops both the suppression and the throwaway initial state.

get_mobdev2_lockdowns() is an async generator, but was annotated
`AsyncIterable`, which has no aclose() -- so the new explicit cleanup in
_create_no_root_tunnel_provider() needed a `# type: ignore`. Annotating
it `AsyncGenerator` makes the call type-check on its own.

Both suppressions were outside what AGENTS.md reserves them for.

userspace_tunnel: Never reach for bonjour on a usbmux miss

The mobdev2 fallback added in #1968 ran implicitly: any command needing a
tunnel would browse the network whenever usbmux had no device for the
requested UDID. That guesses on the user's behalf. A host missing usbmuxd
network support is a host problem, and a device the user did not name
should not be served just because it answered an advert.

It also cost the ordinary case: a paired device that simply is not plugged
in went from failing in 0.2s to 3.2s, on every platform including macOS,
where usbmuxd does its own Wi-Fi discovery and the fallback can never help.

Discovery over bonjour stays available, but only when asked for with
--mobdev2. The incremental browse the fallback was built on
(_browse_receive_loop / iter_browse_service) is kept: it is what makes an
explicit --mobdev2 lookup return in about one mDNS round-trip.

docs: Point Windows users at the iTunes service that sees Wi-Fi devices

Apple's Microsoft Store "Apple Devices" app ships a service that never
discovers devices over Wi-Fi, so an uncabled device simply never appears
in `usbmux list` (its own UI cannot reach the device either, per the
report in #1968). The classic iTunes installer's Apple Mobile Device
Service does, and fixing the host beats working around it.

Recommend it over the Store app where usbmux discovery is explained, and
keep `--mobdev2` as the answer only for hosts that cannot be fixed, such
as Linux, whose stock usbmuxd has the same gap.

bonjour: Stop a browse once the requested device answers

Every lookup aimed at one UDID still sat out the whole bonjour window:
get_mobdev2_devices() drained its generator, and get_rsds() /
get_remote_pairing_tunnel_services() collected all answers before matching
any of them. Since there is exactly one answer worth waiting for, the rest
of the window buys nothing -- a `--mobdev2 --udid X` lookup paid the full
timeout even with the device answering in the first round-trip.

Asking for a specific device now returns as soon as it is found, bounded
by the same timeout. Listing every device is unchanged and still waits the
whole window, because any of them may still be announcing.

iter_browse_remoted/iter_browse_remotepairing join iter_browse_mobdev2 as
the incremental counterparts, and the iter_browse_* family is annotated
AsyncGenerator, which it always was -- AsyncIterable has no aclose(), and
these lookups close their browse in a finally.

userspace_tunnel: Ask RemotePairing for the device we handshook with

The pre-17.4 fallback looked up RemotePairing services with the caller's
serial, which is None whenever a single device is attached and no --udid
was given. Unnamed, the lookup contacts every paired device on the network
and takes services[0] -- so after identifying a device over USB the tunnel
could be built against a different phone, and the services that lost the
race were created and never closed.

The lockdown handshake already names the device, so pass its udid when the
caller did not supply one. An explicit serial still wins. Naming it also
lets the browse stop at that device instead of running to the bonjour
timeout (3s posix / 2s Windows).

doctor: Add a host check for what this machine can reach a device with

"No device found" has too many host-side causes to guess at: usbmuxd not
running, a daemon that cannot discover devices over Wi-Fi, mDNS blocked by
macOS's Local Network privacy setting, no userspace stack installed. Each
was diagnosable only by knowing which internal to call.

`pymobiledevice3 doctor` runs those checks and says what to do about each,
with no device attached -- which is the state being explained. It exits
non-zero when something is broken, and --json gives output worth pasting
into an issue.

Checks prefer proving a capability to inferring it. A device listed over
the network proves Wi-Fi discovery whatever the daemon is; opening one
lockdown connection proves the daemon implements `Connect`, which is what
usbmuxd2 shipped without until 0.64 -- listing worked while every service
connection failed (#1147), the most confusing way this breaks. Daemon
identity is consulted only to explain what could not be exercised, via
OsUtils.usbmux_daemon(): the service registry on Windows tells the Store
"Apple Devices" app apart from the iTunes package, and on Linux only
usbmuxd2 links Avahi.

The mDNS check counts the send errors that arrive through the protocol
rather than the sends attempted, because sendto() reports success on a
host whose queries are all refused.

doctor: Report by capability instead of by internal name

The first report was a flat list of internals: a reader had to know what
"usbmux Wi-Fi discovery" or "mDNS" meant for them before the line helped.

Checks are now named for what someone wants to do, grouped into what works
and what does not, and a failure says what it costs before how to fix it.
A host with nothing wrong says so, rather than leaving the reader to scan
for the absence of a problem.

doctor: Ask the host what is plugged in

"usbmux is not listing it" and "nothing is attached" are the same symptom
with different fixes, and nothing told them apart. On macOS IOKit answers
directly, so ask it (via the ioregistry package, a Darwin-only dependency)
and say "the host sees it, usbmux does not" when the two disagree -- that
is a daemon to restart, not a cable to check.

IOKit spells a modern UDID without the separator usbmux prints, so both
share one normalization.

doctor: Colour the report so the answer is visible at a glance

A wall of uniform text makes the reader find the failing line themselves.
Section headings and each check's title now carry their status colour,
what a failure costs is yellow, and how to fix it is cyan.

Styled in __repr__ rather than in the CLI, so every caller renders a check
the same way, and typer.echo drops the escapes whenever the output is not
a terminal -- piping or redirecting still gives clean text, and --json is
untouched.

doctor: Ask the Linux kernel what is plugged in too

The "host sees it, usbmux does not" verdict was macOS-only, but the
confusion it resolves is at its worst on Linux, where the daemon is the
part most likely to be wrong.

Read /sys/bus/usb/devices for Apple's vendor id rather than shelling out
to lsusb: it is the same data lsusb parses, needs no usbutils install, no
subprocess and no output parsing, and every attribute there is readable
without root. sysfs reports a modern UDID without its separator exactly
as IOKit does, so both share one normalization.

doctor: Report on hosts broken in ways the checks did not expect

Review of the branch found the command failing exactly where it is needed
most, plus a build break.

- mkdocs.yml never listed the new group, so `mkdocs build --strict` aborted
  and the docs workflow would have gone red.
- The "usbmuxd is not reachable" branch filed its remedy as the
  consequence, so the most common failure printed no fix at all, and it
  only caught PyMobileDevice3Exception -- a socket the user cannot open, an
  unresolvable USBMUXD_SOCKET_ADDRESS and a daemon that dies mid-handshake
  all tracebacked instead of being reported.
- Any Apple-vendor USB device counted as an iOS device, so a wired Magic
  Keyboard, a Studio Display or a device in recovery was announced as
  "usbmux does not see it", with the wrong fix and a non-zero exit on a
  healthy host. Serials must now be UDID-shaped, and are compared the way
  usbmux compares them rather than by rebuilding its spelling.
- The connect probe took the first listed device, usually the Wi-Fi entry,
  and usbmux has no timeout of its own -- a sleeping device hung the whole
  command. It now prefers the USB link and bounds the wait.
- The tunneld check connected an RSD to every tunnelled device, and mapped
  every possible failure to "not running". It now only lists them, through
  a new get_tunneld_tunnels(), and the HTTP call that had no timeout has
  one.
- Pair records counted remote_*.plist twice, since both kinds share a
  folder.
- Every check is now guarded: an unexpected exception becomes one line
  instead of costing the report and every later check.
- Windows ImagePath is parsed properly -- it is REG_EXPAND_SZ, may carry
  arguments, and an unquoted path may contain spaces. Linux daemon
  identification falls back to the on-disk binary, since /proc/<pid>/maps
  of a root-owned usbmuxd is unreadable for the user actually running this.

cli_common.isatty() no longer raises on a stdout without a file
descriptor, which is what made every --json command untestable through
CliRunner; --json now also carries the environment line and honours the
same exit code as the text report.

doctor: Drop the ioregistry cast now that it ships types

ioregistry 0.0.6 ships py.typed (doronz88/ioregistry#6), so its already
annotated API is finally visible to pyright. The property read here no
longer needs a cast or a rule suppression to stay clean, and the floor
records why the older release will not do.

doctor: Describe the attached device, and ask for the report in issues

Host facts alone do not explain a command that works on one device and
fails on another, and the two commonest causes of "the tunnel is up but
`developer` still fails" are invisible from the host: developer mode off,
or no developer disk image mounted.

When a device is reachable the report now names it -- model, OS version,
whether it is paired -- then reports developer mode (iOS 16+, where the
concept begins) and whether the right image type is mounted, Personalized
from iOS 17 and Developer before it. Each says what it costs and the
command that fixes it.

It never pairs: the lockdown connection is opened with autopair=False, so
running a diagnostic cannot pop a trust dialog on someone's device, and an
unpaired device is reported as the fact it is.

The bug report template now asks for this output instead of asking people
to list host OS, Python, versions and device details by hand -- it carries
all of that, plus what the host can actually reach.

doctor: Derive the rules it reports on instead of restating them

A report that drifts from the code it describes is worse than no report,
because people believe it. Two rules were stated twice.

Which developer image a device uses was decided independently here and in
auto_mount(); when that cutoff moves, mounting would follow it and the
report would not. uses_personalized_image() / image_type_for_device() are
now the one place it is decided, and auto_mount() dispatches on the same
predicate.

"No mDNS query could leave this host" was copied out of bonjour with a
different settle window, so the browse warning and the report could
already disagree under load. bonjour now exposes probe_multicast() and
is_multicast_blocked(), used by both, and doctor no longer reaches into
its privates at all.

Both are pinned by tests that fail on divergence rather than on a
particular answer, including one asserting doctor imports no bonjour
internals -- the next person to need one should add a public helper.

The report is also split into Host and Device. They answer different
questions, and someone fixing one should not have to sift the other; the
JSON carries the same scope per check.

doctor: Pin the last restated rule and the advice it gives

Two things could still drift into being confidently wrong.

Whether a device has a developer mode at all was decided independently by
the mounter, which refuses to mount without it, and by the report. It now
lives once on LockdownServiceProvider beside product_version, and both ask
it. The test fake borrows that property rather than reimplementing it --
a fake that restates the rule could not catch the rule moving.

The hints name real commands to run, and a rename would turn help into
wrong instructions with nothing failing. Every `pymobiledevice3 ...` string
in the module is now resolved against the CLI, parsed out of string
literals via ast so an import line is not mistaken for advice. Verified it
fails when a command is renamed.

doctor: Check daemon identification against a real usbmuxd in CI

Every platform path here is unit tested over fakes, which cannot catch the
thing most likely to be wrong: what a real daemon looks like on disk and in
/proc. A job on ubuntu-latest installs stock usbmuxd and asserts the doctor
identifies it, and runs the report once to prove it does not crash on a
host that has a daemon but no device. Nothing here needs a device --
identifying the daemon is about the daemon.

Also corrects the Wi-Fi hint, which implied enabling the setting was
sufficient. Reach is per host: a device advertises one authentication tag
per paired host, so a machine that has never been cabled to it cannot
recognise it however the setting is set.

docs: Separate a device that is advertising from a host that has listed it

"Wi-Fi is enabled but the device is missing" has two unrelated causes and
only one of them is on the device. EnableWifiConnections applies the moment
it is written -- verified against a device, where the advert disappears and
returns within seconds of writing it -- so re-running `wifi-connections on`
when the browse already finds the device changes nothing, and the daemon
that has not listed it is the host's.

Documents the split, the cheap ways to make the host re-discover, and
`com.apple.mobile.lockdown.BonjourServiceChanged`: lockdownd observes that
notification, drops its wireless connections and re-registers the Bonjour
service, and posts it to itself after pair records change. Posting it
changes no setting.

Also repeats that Wi-Fi reach is per host, since arriving here from a
working machine and finding a second one blind is the usual way this is
met.

doctor: Skip the sysfs tree test where its node names are illegal

A realistic fake sysfs tree needs an interface node beside the device node,
and those are named like 1-1:1.0. Windows rejects ':' in a path, so the
fixture could not build the tree there at all -- and the code it covers
reads /sys, which Windows does not have either.

doctor: Stop the browse-window assertion tripping on a coarse clock

The listing test asserted it sat out a 0.2s window, against a Windows
clock that rounds to ~16ms and undershot by 12ms. Asserting most of the
window rather than all of it survives that, and still fails when the
lookup returns at the first answer -- verified by reintroducing exactly
that regression.

tunneld: Deflake federation tests on Windows by draining the bridge

test_connect_picks_the_tunnel_the_client_named kept failing on the Windows
runners with two unraisable exceptions at teardown:

- StreamWriters GC'd while their transports were still closing. They were

  synchronously, so the test's event loop could end first. Wait for the
  pumps to finish and let the loop run the closes it scheduled, as
  test_tunneld_remote_bridge already does.

native_tunnel: Close the CLI's session at exit instead of crashing

The CLI's atexit hook closed its native tunnel through aclose(), whose
asyncio.to_thread() is refused once interpreter shutdown has begun
("can't register atexit after shutdown"). The error was suppressed, so the
session was never closed: the device kept the tunnel assertion, and
remotepairingd kept delivering events to the connections' ctypes handlers
while the interpreter finalized. Taking the GIL for one then crashed the
process with SIGSEGV in PyGILState_Ensure, after the command itself had
succeeded -- most runs of `mounter auto-mount`, which now retries over the
native tunnel by default on macOS.

Close the session on the exiting thread instead.

native_tunnel: Wait for each cancelled connection to invalidate

xpc_connection_cancel() is asynchronous: libxpc still delivers a final
XPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_INVALID to the connection's handler afterwards, on a
libdispatch thread. Closing from the atexit hook, that event can still
reach the Python handler while the interpreter finalizes. Wait for it,
bounded so a wedged daemon cannot hang exit; nothing reaches the handler
after it. The per-device connection's handler now records it too.

mounter: Exit non-zero when no image could be mounted

`mounter auto-mount` caught its own failures -- an unwritable Xcode path,
no image for the iOS version, a failed download -- logged them and
returned, so the process exited 0 and scripts treated a failed mount as a
success. Exit 1 for those instead. The explicit mount and unmount commands
now exit 1 on the errors catch_errors logs too.

An image that is already mounted is what auto-mount was asked for, so that
still exits 0, now logged at info rather than as an error: scripts that
auto-mount before every run must not start failing on their second run.

remotexpc: Treat EOF at a frame header as a terminated connection

_recvall turns EOF inside a frame body into ConnectionTerminatedError,
but _receive_frame read the header with a bare readexactly(). When the
peer closed the connection between frames -- as cryptexd does when it
crashes mid-install -- the IncompleteReadError escaped instead, and since
it is an EOFError, the CLI reported nothing but "Aborted.". Read the
header through _recvall too.

cryptexd: Explain an install that cryptexd dropped

When cryptexd rejects an install badly enough to crash, it closes the
connection without replying. Raise CryptexdError saying so, and pointing
at its device log, instead of a bare terminated connection.

cryptexd: Only install the DeveloperDiskImage cryptex from iOS 26.4

cryptex auto-install crashed cryptexd on iOS 26.0.1 (#1991). Read from
the firmware, two things change between 26.3.1 and 26.4 and match 27.0
from 26.4 on:

- The platform sandbox profile's rule for cryptex mounts. Below 26.4,
  cryptexd imports a Cryptex1 image but the kernel denies it mounting one
  at /System/Developer, the DDI's RequiredMountPath: with the asset type
  fixed, 26.0.1 still failed with "deny(1) file-mount /System/Developer".
- The asset type table that image-type-index indexes, whose "root" entry
  26.4 split in two. Below it DDI_IMAGE_TYPE_INDEX names
  Cryptex1,GenericVolume instead of GenericDmg, which is what crashed
  cryptexd: "asset already present: Cryptex1,GenericVolume".

So iOS installs the DDI as a cryptex only from 26.4; below it the image
mounter's PersonalizedDMG is the way, as mounter auto-mount does. Refuse
there before asking Apple to sign anything, and point at auto-mount.

remotexpc: Identify as remoted only on links remoted uses

Since 11.15.5 every RSD handshake on macOS presented the host remoted's
UUID. From iOS 26.2 the device keeps one RSD connection per peer UUID, so
on a tunnel of our own such a handshake still evicts remoted's connection
("Device connection interrupted" in remoted's log); remoted redials a
second later with the same UUID and evicts ours:

    $ pymobiledevice3 remote rsd-info --rsd fd73:a27a:4596::1 52456
    ConnectionResetError: [Errno 54] Connection reset by peer

After a few rounds remoted stops redialing, and Xcode/devicectl lose the
device until remoted restarts.

Identify with the deterministic host id by default instead. It is still
one stable UUID per host, which is all iOS 27.2's re-attach needs from
connections sharing a tunnel. On links remoted itself uses -- the USB NCM
interface (get_rsds, tunneld, get_remoted_devices) and remoted's own
tunnel (the native tunnel) -- keep presenting remoted's UUID, via the new
remoted_handshake_uuid: remoted is the peer the device remembers there,
and a different UUID makes iOS 27.2 reset the tunnel service we open.

cli: Default to the userspace tunnel on macOS

The native tunnel rides the host remoted's own tunnel, on which the device
keeps a single RSD connection. The native tunnel's connection evicts
remoted's ("Device connection interrupted" in remoted's log), and remoted
redials and evicts ours back, whatever UUID we present. Commands fail
intermittently with ConnectionResetError/ConnectionRefusedError, and after a
few rounds remoted stops redialing, so Xcode/devicectl lose the device until
remoted restarts (#1994).

The userspace tunnel brings up a tunnel of its own, which nothing else on the
host competes for: with remoted attached, repeated sessions on an iOS 27.2
device all succeeded and remoted was never interrupted. Make it the built-in
default on macOS, as it already is elsewhere. --native and
PYMOBILEDEVICE3_DEFAULT_FALLBACK=native still select the native tunnel, and
it remains the no-root fallback for iOS 17.0-17.3, which userspace cannot
serve.

`remote start-tunnel` follows the preference, so it builds the classic
tunnel by default again. `remote browse` keeps asking remotepairingd on
macOS, since browsing opens no RSD connection.

rsd_tunnel: Prefer the userspace tunnel on macOS

PreferredRsdTunnel tried the native tunnel first on macOS, so library
callers hit the same eviction fight with remoted as the CLI did (#1994).
Use the userspace tunnel, as the CLI now does, and fall back to the
native tunnel on macOS only when the userspace tunnel cannot serve the
device (iOS 17.0-17.3). prefer_native=True keeps the old order.

docs: Describe the userspace tunnel as the default on macOS

The native tunnel is opt-in now, and it does not coexist with remoted as
the docs claimed: on remoted's tunnel the device keeps a single RSD
connection, which ours and remoted's keep evicting from each other
(#1994). Update the guides, AGENTS.md and the device-operator skill,
and say what the native tunnel costs where it is offered.

remotexpc: Document the device's RSD peer rules
